evangelical.abortion: Evangelicals typically treat abortion as the taking of innocent human life and a grave moral evil, much as the Church does. They usually ground this in Scripture and the image of God rather than in natural-law manuals or Magisterial documents. They have no analogue to formal cooperation, latae sententiae penalties, or the canonical crime of abortion; the emphasis is personal sin, repentance, and political opposition.
ortho.abortion: Eastern Orthodox teaching, like Catholic teaching, regards abortion as the killing of a human being and a grave sin from conception. They frame it less in Scholastic natural-law terms and more as a wound to the image of God and a failure of ascesis and mercy. They do not use the Latin distinction of mortal and venial sin or automatic excommunication, but they treat it as requiring Confession and a serious penance.
protestant.abortion: Historic Protestant bodies generally condemn abortion as contrary to the commandment against murder, overlapping the Catholic judgment that it is the taking of innocent life. Many mainline Protestants today are more internally divided than Catholics or Evangelicals. They lack a single Magisterium, so there is no binding equivalent of Evangelium vitae; discipline varies by denomination.
adventist.alcohol: Adventists usually require total abstinence from alcohol as part of a health message tied to the body as the temple of the Holy Spirit. This is stricter than Catholic temperance, which permits moderate use of wine. They do not treat wine in the Eucharist as Catholics do; Communion is typically unfermented grape juice.
holiness.alcohol: Holiness churches often bind members to total abstinence as a mark of entire sanctification and separation from the world. Catholic temperance allows moderate drinking; Holiness ethics treat alcohol itself as a near occasion to be refused. The concern is holiness of life more than a shared sacramental use of wine.
lds.alcohol: Latter-day Saints forbid alcohol under the Word of Wisdom, a health and obedience covenant. This is not the Catholic virtue of temperance but a revealed dietary law. Wine is not used as the matter of their sacrament; water is used instead.
protestant.alcohol: Protestants range from Lutheran and Anglican comfort with wine, including in the Lord's Supper, to Evangelical and Holiness abstinence. Catholic teaching names temperance a cardinal virtue and uses wine as necessary matter for the Eucharist. Many Protestants treat the question as adiaphora unless it becomes drunkenness.
baptist.altar_call: Baptists often invite hearers to come forward to profess faith or request baptism. This is not a sacrament and does not map onto an altar of sacrifice; the 'altar' is a revival-meeting image. Catholics look for conversion in Baptism, Confession, and a formed act of contrition, not a public walk forward as the decisive moment.
evangelical.altar_call: Evangelicals use the altar call as a ritual of decision: repent and accept Christ now. It functions as an external prompt to conversion, but it is not Confession, not a sacrament, and not the Catholic altar. Assurance is often tied to that moment of coming forward rather than to sacramental grace.
pentecostal.altar_call: Pentecostals combine the invitation with prayer for salvation, healing, or Spirit baptism at the front of the church. The space is a place of encounter, not the Catholic altar of the Eucharistic sacrifice. Tongues, slaying in the Spirit, and altar ministry have no direct Catholic sacramental counterpart.
adventist.annihilation: Adventists commonly teach conditional immortality: the lost are finally destroyed, not endlessly tormented. This rejects the Catholic doctrine of hell as eternal punishment of the damned. They often deny a naturally immortal soul, so eternal death means cessation rather than the eternal loss of the beatific vision.
jehovahs_witnesses.annihilation: Jehovah's Witnesses teach that Gehenna means annihilation, not eternal conscious torment. They deny the immortal soul as Catholics understand it. The wicked cease to exist; there is no hell of everlasting punishment and no purgatory.
ortho.annihilation: Eastern Orthodox generally affirm eternal punishment and reject annihilationism, sharing the Catholic conviction that hell is real and unending. They more often describe hell as the experience of God's love as fire by those who reject Him, rather than as a purely forensic sentence. They do not define the metaphysics of the soul in Latin Scholastic terms.
protestant.annihilation: Classical Protestant confessions taught eternal conscious punishment, close to Catholic hell. A growing minority holds conditional immortality. There is no Magisterium to settle the question; hell in Protestant use may mean either everlasting torment or final destruction.
ortho.anointing_of_the_sick: Orthodox Holy Unction is a Mystery for healing of soul and body, comparable to the sacrament of Anointing of the Sick. It is often celebrated for groups and not reserved to the dying, a pastoral range Catholics also recovered after Vatican II. They do not use the older Latin name Extreme Unction as the ordinary title.
pentecostal.anointing_of_the_sick: Pentecostals anoint with oil following James 5, expecting charismatic healing. This is a prayer ordinance, not a sacrament conferring grace ex opere operato. There is no reserved matter, form, or priestly minister as in Catholic Anointing.
protestant.anointing_of_the_sick: Many Protestants will anoint the sick as a biblical practice of prayer. It is not one of seven sacraments. Healing is asked of God; the rite does not itself confer sacramental grace as Catholic Anointing does.
anglican.apocrypha: Anglicans typically print the deuterocanonical books as Apocrypha, useful for example of life but not to establish doctrine (Article VI). Catholics receive those books as fully canonical Scripture. Apocrypha in Anglican usage therefore names what Catholics call deuterocanonical.
ortho.apocrypha: Orthodox read a slightly larger set of books than the Catholic deuterocanon as anagignoskomena—readable in church. They are Scripture in liturgical life, though Orthodox sometimes hesitate to use Catholic language of a closed Tridentine list. The overlap with the Catholic canon is large.
protestant.apocrypha: Most Protestants exclude the deuterocanonical books from the canon and may call them Apocrypha. Catholics hold them as inspired Scripture defined at Trent. Protestants do not treat Tobit, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, or the Maccabees as binding for dogma.
lds.apostles_today: Latter-day Saints have a living Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and a First Presidency with keys they believe were restored after a total apostasy. This is not apostolic succession by episcopal ordination as Catholics understand it. Apostle is a present governing office, not only the Twelve of the New Testament age.
new_apostolic.apostles_today: The New Apostolic Church is led by living apostles, with a Chief Apostle at the head. They claim continuing apostolic ministry as necessary for valid sealing and salvation. Catholics hold that public revelation ended with the death of the last Apostle and that bishops succeed the Apostles in office, not as a new college of apostles.
pentecostal.apostles_today: Some Pentecostals teach a restored fivefold ministry, including apostles who plant churches and exercise extra-local authority. This is charismatic office, not Holy Orders in apostolic succession. Catholics do not recognize a revived apostolic office alongside the episcopate.
protestant.apostles_today: Most Protestants hold that the apostolic office ceased with the original Apostles. Ministry continues through pastors, elders, or bishops without claiming to be apostles. This is closer to the Catholic sense that there are no new Apostles, though Protestants usually reject Catholic apostolic succession.
anglican.apostolic_succession: Anglicans claim historic episcopal succession and often treat it as of the esse or at least the bene esse of the Church. Leo XIII in Apostolicae curae judged Anglican orders invalid; many Anglicans contest that judgment. Their language of succession sounds Catholic but is not recognized as such by Rome.
lds.apostolic_succession: Latter-day Saints speak of priesthood succession through restored keys given to Joseph Smith by heavenly messengers, not through an unbroken line of bishops from the Apostles. Catholics would call this a claim of new revelation rather than apostolic succession. They believe Catholic succession was lost in the Great Apostasy.
oriental_ortho.apostolic_succession: Oriental Orthodox churches maintain episcopal succession from the Apostles through their patriarchates, as Catholics do. They do not accept later councils that Catholics and Eastern Orthodox share after Ephesus or Chalcedon, depending on the church. Succession is real in their own hierarchy; communion with Rome is lacking.
ortho.apostolic_succession: Eastern Orthodox hold apostolic succession through Orthodox bishops in communion with the Orthodox Church. They deny that succession can be reduced to a pipeline of rites apart from Orthodox faith and communion. Catholics recognize Orthodox orders as valid; Orthodox typically do not treat Catholic bishops as simply equivalent.
protestant.apostolic_succession: Most Protestants reject succession of bishops as necessary for a true church. Authority rests in Scripture and the call of the congregation or presbytery. Apostolic means fidelity to apostolic teaching, not an unbroken laying-on of hands.
lds.ascension: Latter-day Saints affirm that the risen Christ ascended and has a glorified body of flesh and bone. They also teach appearances and ministry in the Americas after the Resurrection, which Catholics do not receive as public revelation. The Ascension itself is confessed, but the wider narrative of Christ's post-resurrection work differs.
ortho.ascension: Orthodox celebrate the Ascension as a great feast: the human nature of Christ is enthroned at the right hand of the Father. This matches Catholic dogma. The liturgical and iconographic emphasis is very strong; the doctrine is the same mystery Catholics confess in the Creed.
protestant.ascension: Protestants confess the Ascension as a biblical event and article of the Creed. They rarely develop it as a liturgical season with the density of Catholic or Orthodox feasts. Doctrinally it is the same confession that Christ bodily ascended and will return.
evangelical.assurance: Evangelicals often teach that a believer can and should know he is saved, sometimes from a conversion experience or the inner witness of the Spirit. Catholics speak of the hope of salvation and reject an absolute certainty of final perseverance apart from special revelation. Assurance in Evangelical use is stronger than Catholic certainty of hope.
ortho.assurance: Orthodox are cautious about claiming certainty of salvation, stressing synergy, repentance, and the fear of God. This is pastorally close to Catholic resistance to presumption. They do not use the Reformation language of assurance of faith as a mark of true belief.
reformed.assurance: Reformed theology treats assurance as ordinarily attainable through faith, the fruit of the Spirit, and the promises of the covenant, while warning against false security. It is not the Catholic virtue of hope plus examination of conscience, nor Evangelical once-saved-always-saved in every case. Perseverance of the saints undergirds the possibility of assurance.
ortho.assumption: Orthodox celebrate the Dormition of the Theotokos: Mary died, her soul was received by Christ, and her body was taken into heaven. Catholics define the Assumption; whether Mary died is left open. The mystery is shared; the defined Latin dogma and the word Assumption are not Orthodox technical terms.
oriental_ortho.assumption: Oriental Orthodox keep the Dormition as a major feast, teaching Mary's holy death and translation to glory. They do not depend on the 1950 papal definition. The content is close to Catholic faith in Mary's bodily glorification.
protestant.assumption: Most Protestants do not teach the Assumption or Dormition as doctrine. Mary died like other believers and awaits the resurrection. They see the Catholic dogma as extra-biblical Tradition.
christian_science.atonement: Christian Science reads atonement as at-one-ment: awakening from the illusion of sin and matter rather than a sacrificial satisfaction. This does not map onto Catholic satisfaction, merit, or the sacrifice of the Cross. Jesus demonstrates divine sonship; Calvary is not propitiatory in the Catholic sense.
lds.atonement: Latter-day Saints place the Atonement in Gethsemane and on the Cross, with Christ taking our pains in the garden as well as dying. It enables resurrection for all and exaltation for the faithful. Catholic theology centers the sacrifice on the Cross and does not treat Gethsemane as coequal locus of vicarious suffering in the same way.
ortho.atonement: Orthodox emphasize Christus Victor, healing, and the destruction of death more than Anselmian satisfaction. They do not deny the Cross as redemptive; they resist reducing it to a legal payment. Catholic language of satisfaction and merit is Latin and is not the Orthodox first vocabulary.
protestant.atonement: Many Protestants, especially Evangelicals, teach penal substitution: Christ bears the penalty of sin in our place. Catholics can speak of vicarious satisfaction but do not typically say the Father punishes the Son as a substitute under retributive wrath in the Reformed sense. Atonement is shared; the mechanism is disputed.
reformed.atonement: Reformed theology classically teaches penal substitution and, in many confessions, limited atonement—Christ died efficaciously for the elect. Catholics teach that Christ died for all, with the fruit applied variously. Limited atonement has no Catholic counterpart as a dogma.
evangelical.baptism_in_the_spirit: Evangelicals may speak of being filled with the Spirit as empowerment for holiness and witness, sometimes subsequent to conversion. This is not Confirmation and not a distinct sacrament. Catholics might analogize it to actual graces or charismatic renewal, not to a second necessary work.
holiness.baptism_in_the_spirit: Holiness churches often identify a second blessing of entire sanctification with Spirit baptism. Catholic sanctifying grace and growth in holiness are not concentrated into one crisis experience after conversion. Second blessing does not map onto a sacrament.
lds.baptism_in_the_spirit: Latter-day Saints speak of the baptism of fire and of the Holy Ghost after water baptism, often associated with confirmation by the laying on of hands. The pattern resembles Baptism plus Confirmation, but the authority claimed is restored priesthood keys, not Catholic Holy Orders.
oneness_pentecostal.baptism_in_the_spiri: Oneness Pentecostals require Spirit baptism evidenced by speaking in tongues as part of the new-birth plan of salvation with repentance and Jesus-name baptism. Catholics do not treat tongues as necessary evidence of the Spirit or as required for justification. Their Holy Ghost baptism is not Confirmation.
pentecostal.baptism_in_the_spirit: Classical Pentecostals teach a distinct baptism in the Holy Spirit after conversion, usually evidenced by tongues. Catholics receive the Spirit in Baptism and Confirmation; later infillings are graces, not a required third sacrament. The Pentecostal crisis experience is not the Catholic sacramental economy.
baptist.baptism: Baptists practice believer's baptism by immersion as an ordinance that confesses an already received salvation. It is not a sacrament that regenerates or remits original sin in the Catholic sense. Infant baptism is rejected; baptism does not incorporate in the way Catholic Baptism does.
churches_of_christ.baptism: Churches of Christ teach baptism by immersion for the remission of sins as necessary to becoming a Christian. This is closer to Catholic instrumental causality than Baptist memorialism, yet they deny infant baptism, original sin as Catholics define it, and baptism as a sacrament in a sevenfold system.
lds.baptism: Latter-day Saints baptize by immersion from the age of accountability (eight) for remission of sins, by proper priesthood authority. They also baptize vicariously for the dead. Catholic Baptism is given to infants, is not repeated, and has no proxy rite for the deceased.
oneness_pentecostal.baptism: Oneness Pentecostals baptize by immersion in the name of Jesus Christ only, not the Trinitarian formula. Catholics require baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit for validity. Their Jesus-name baptism is tied to a non-Trinitarian view of God.
ortho.baptism: Orthodox Baptism is a Mystery of triple immersion, regeneration, and union with Christ, followed immediately by Chrismation and Communion even for infants. Catholics recognize Orthodox Baptism as valid. The theology of regeneration is shared; the ordinary rite and the immediate completion of Christian initiation differ from Latin practice.
protestant.baptism: Protestants agree baptism is commanded but divide on whether it is a sacrament of regeneration, a covenant sign, or a believer's testimony. Catholics teach baptismal regeneration and infant baptism as ordinary. Ordinance language signals a weaker causal claim than Catholic sacrament.
anabaptist.infant_baptism: Anabaptists reject infant baptism as invalid and baptize only confessing believers. Catholic infant baptism is, for them, no baptism at all. Church membership begins with adult decision, not with the faith of the Church supplying for the child.
baptist.infant_baptism: Baptists hold credobaptism only. An infant cannot make the required profession of faith. Catholic teaching that Baptism remits original sin in infants is denied; dedication rites may replace christening.
lutheran.infant_baptism: Lutherans baptize infants and typically teach that baptism works forgiveness of sins and gives the Spirit. This is much closer to Catholic baptismal regeneration than Baptist practice. They do not require Catholic confirmation of the rite's validity questions in the same canonical frame.
ortho.infant_baptism: Orthodox baptize infants and immediately chrismate and communicate them. Catholics share infant baptism; the full initiation of infants at the font is the older Eastern pattern, now also visible in Catholic Eastern churches.
reformed.infant_baptism: Reformed churches baptize infants as covenant children, a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, not always as regenerative in the Catholic ex opere operato sense. The analogue is more circumcision than Catholic instrumental regeneration, though some Reformed speak strongly of baptismal grace.
adventist.church_and_state: Adventists historically stress religious liberty and suspicion of church-state union, shaped by a reading of apocalyptic prophecy about persecuting powers. Catholics also teach religious freedom after Dignitatis humanae, but Adventist narrative often identified historic Catholicism with oppressive union of throne and altar.
baptist.church_and_state: Baptists classically teach separation of church and state and soul liberty. This overlaps Catholic religious freedom but historically opposed Catholic establishment. The state has no competence to enforce baptism or dogma.
lds.church_and_state: Latter-day Saints officially teach political neutrality of the Church as an institution while expecting members to be civic participants. Early Utah theocracy is not the present model. There is no Catholic doctrine of the two powers in the Gelasian sense as their current official frame.
ortho.church_and_state: Orthodox historically describe symphony between emperor and Church rather than the Western medieval tension of two swords. In modern nations the pattern varies. Catholics will hear an analogue to establishment, not the American Baptist wall of separation.
protestant.church_and_state: Protestants range from magisterial establishment to radical separation. There is no single doctrine. Catholic social teaching now affirms freedom of religion while still seeing the Church as a public society, not a private club.
amish.church_discipline: The Amish practice Meidung, or shunning, of members under the ban. This is a stricter social exclusion than typical Catholic excommunication, which bars from the sacraments but not necessarily from family table. The Ordnung, not canon law, is the rule.
anabaptist.church_discipline: Anabaptists use the ban to keep the church a visible community of saints. Catholic discipline aims at medicinal recovery through penalties and Penance. The Anabaptist goal is a pure gathered church more than a mixed body of sinners and saints.
lds.church_discipline: Latter-day Saints convene membership councils that can restrict privileges or withdraw membership. Analogues are canonical penalties, but the forum is local priesthood leadership, not a Catholic tribunal. Temple worthiness adds a layer Catholics do not have.
protestant.church_discipline: Protestants may excommunicate or remove members for unrepentant sin. Practice is uneven. There is no unified Code of Canon Law; the Catholic medicinal and juridical system is more formal.
anglican.closed_communion: Anglican practice ranges from open hospitality to more restricted altar fellowship. Catholics require Catholic communion in full communion, with limited exceptions. Many Anglicans invite all baptized Christians; that is broader than Catholic closed communion.
baptist.closed_communion: Some Baptists practice close or closed communion, limiting the Table to baptized believers of like faith, sometimes only the local church. The concern is church purity and believer's baptism, not Catholic eucharistic communion and orders.
lutheran.closed_communion: Confessional Lutherans practice closed communion or altar fellowship based on doctrinal agreement. This resembles Catholic closed communion in restricting the sacrament, but the criterion is shared confession rather than communion with the successor of Peter.
ortho.closed_communion: Orthodox communion is closed to those in Orthodox communion, very much as Catholic communion is closed. Orthodox generally do not admit Catholics, despite Catholic recognition of Orthodox mysteries. The principle of communion ecclesiology is shared; the boundary of the Church is not.
protestant.closed_communion: Many Protestants practice open communion for all who profess faith in Christ. That contradicts Catholic discipline. Open communion means the Lord's Supper is not restricted by denominational membership.
community_of_christ.degrees_of_glory: Community of Christ inherited language of degrees of glory but has moved toward more conventional Christian eschatology and does not emphasize three kingdoms as LDS doctrine does. Catholics confess one heaven of the beatific vision, not graded kingdoms of glory.
lds.degrees_of_glory: Latter-day Saints teach celestial, terrestrial, and telestial kingdoms, plus outer darkness. This does not map onto heaven, purgatory, and hell. Almost all are saved into some glory; exaltation in the celestial kingdom is the analogue to the highest union with God, not the beatific vision as Catholics define it.
protestant.degrees_of_glory: Protestants typically teach one heaven and one hell, not degrees of glory as kingdoms. Some speak of rewards, which Catholics can analogize to degrees of blessedness in heaven, not to separate worlds after death.
adventist.food_laws: Adventists often avoid unclean meats of Leviticus and promote vegetarianism as part of the health message. Catholics hold that the ceremonial law is fulfilled and all foods are clean, with fasting as ascetic discipline, not kosher classification.
jehovahs_witnesses.food_laws: Jehovah's Witnesses require abstinence from blood, including blood transfusions, reading Acts 15 as a standing law. Catholics do not treat transfusion as eating blood. The Witness rule functions as a binding discipline far beyond Catholic dietary fasts.
lds.food_laws: The Word of Wisdom forbids alcohol, tobacco, coffee, and tea and commends grains and moderation in meat. It is covenant obedience, not Catholic abstinence days. Coffee and tea have no Catholic moral prohibition.
messianic.food_laws: Messianic believers often keep kashrut as discipleship to Yeshua the Jew. Catholics see Mosaic food laws as not binding on the Church. Torah observance here is identity and holiness, not sacrament.
protestant.food_laws: Most Protestants quote Mark 7 and Acts 10: all foods clean. Fasting may be practiced but not as unclean versus clean. This agrees with Catholic freedom from kosher law, though Catholic Friday abstinence is a church discipline Protestants usually drop.
adventist.great_apostasy: Adventists speak of a falling away in which Sunday sacredness and other errors entered the Church, often implicating papal Rome. Catholics teach indefectibility: the Church cannot fail in her essential faith. Apostasy in Adventist prophecy is a historical narrative Catholics reject.
jehovahs_witnesses.great_apostasy: Jehovah's Witnesses teach that after the Apostles the Church became apostate until their modern restoration. This denies Catholic apostolic continuity. The Catholic Church is not, for them, the surviving Church of the Creed.
lds.great_apostasy: Latter-day Saints teach a Great Apostasy so complete that priesthood keys left the earth until the Restoration. Catholics hold that the gates of hell do not prevail and succession never failed. The two claims are direct contradictions.
ortho.great_apostasy: Orthodox deny that the Church failed. They may accuse Rome of falling into error without teaching a total apostasy of the kind restorationists claim. Indefectibility of the Church is shared in substance with Catholics, located in Orthodoxy.
restorationist.great_apostasy: Restorationists generally hold that the New Testament church was lost or obscured and must be restored from Scripture. Catholic indefectibility rules that out. Falling away is read as institutional ruin, not merely sin among members.
adventist.investigative_judgment: Adventists teach that since 1844 Christ has been conducting an investigative judgment in the heavenly sanctuary, reviewing professed believers. Catholics have particular and general judgment, not a pre-Advent investigative phase begun in 1844. The heavenly sanctuary doctrine is foreign to Catholic eschatology.
protestant.investigative_judgment: Most Protestants reject the investigative judgment as an Adventist distinctive without biblical warrant. Judgment is at death and/or at the coming of Christ. There is no 1844 heavenly turning point.
seventh_day_adventist.investigative_judg: Seventh-day Adventists make the investigative judgment and heavenly sanctuary central. It explains the delayed Advent after 1844. Catholics would classify this as a new doctrinal system, not a development of the Creed.
adventist.intermediate_state: Many Adventists teach that the dead sleep unconsciously until the resurrection. There is no Catholic particular judgment with the soul at the vision of God or in hell or purgatory. Prayers for the dead and invocation of saints are excluded by soul sleep.
lds.intermediate_state: Latter-day Saints teach a spirit world divided into paradise and prison, where the gospel may be preached to the dead. This is more populated and missionary than Catholic waiting after death. It underwrites baptism for the dead, which Catholics reject.
ortho.intermediate_state: Orthodox teach particular judgment and a waiting state; some popular teaching mentions toll-houses. They reject purgatory as a Latin satisfaction system but pray for the departed. The analogue to purgatory is imperfect; the analogue to particular judgment is close.
protestant.intermediate_state: Protestants often say the believer is immediately with the Lord, the lost in Hades or hell, with no purgatory. Some hold soul sleep. Catholic purification after death is denied by most.
adventist.last_judgment: Adventists include a pre-Advent investigative phase and a millennial review before the final destruction of the wicked. Catholic Last Judgment is a single public judgment at the resurrection. The timeline and sanctuary imagery differ.
lds.last_judgment: Latter-day Saints teach a final judgment assigning degrees of glory. Catholic judgment separates saved and lost for heaven or hell after any purgation. Graded kingdoms replace the simpler Catholic two-fold eternal outcome plus purgatory.
ortho.last_judgment: Orthodox confess the Last Judgment as in the Creed and icons of the Parousia. The doctrine matches Catholic general judgment. Emphasis is iconic and liturgical more than Scholastic.
protestant.last_judgment: Protestants confess a final judgment according to the Gospel. Details of millennium and rapture split them. The core is compatible with Catholic general judgment, minus purgatory and usually minus particular-judgment precision.
adventist.millennium: Adventists typically teach that the millennium is spent by the redeemed in heaven while the earth is desolate, after which the wicked are raised and destroyed. Catholic amillennial tradition reads the thousand years as the age of the Church. The empty-earth millennium is not Catholic.
evangelical.millennium: Evangelicals divide into pre-, post-, and amillennial camps. Dispensational premillennialism is common. Catholics generally reject a coming earthly millennial kingdom of the kind chiliasts describe.
jehovahs_witnesses.millennium: Jehovah's Witnesses teach a literal thousand-year reign of Christ with the 144,000 from heaven over a paradise earth. This is a specific restorationist millennialism. Catholic eschatology does not include a two-class heaven/earth split of that kind.
lds.millennium: Latter-day Saints expect a literal Millennium on earth with Christ reigning, temple work continuing, and Satan bound. Catholics do not teach ongoing proxy ordinances in a millennial earthly church. The hope of a renewed earth exists in Catholic new creation, without LDS temple cosmology.
protestant.millennium: Protestant views vary widely. Confessional Reformed and Lutheran thought is often amillennial, closer to Catholic reading of Revelation 20. Popular Protestantism may be premillennial.
adventist.rapture: Adventists reject a secret pre-tribulation rapture. Christ returns visibly once. This agrees with Catholic rejection of a secret rapture, though the rest of Adventist apocalyptic does not.
evangelical.rapture: Many Evangelicals teach a rapture of the Church distinct from the glorious appearing, often before tribulation. Catholics do not teach a two-stage coming that removes the Church from history while the world continues. 1 Thessalonians 4 is read as the one Parousia.
protestant.rapture: Some Protestants use rapture simply for being caught up at the one coming of Christ; others mean a secret removal. Catholic teaching knows one visible return. The word itself is not Catholic technical vocabulary.
adventist.restoration: Adventists see themselves as a remnant restoring neglected truths—Sabbath, sanctuary, state of the dead. Catholics see no lost public revelation to restore. Remnant language claims a prophetic identity the Magisterium does not grant them.
churches_of_christ.restoration: Churches of Christ seek to restore the New Testament church in name, ordinance, and organization, rejecting creeds. Catholic apostolic continuity denies that the Church disappeared. Restoration is a hermeneutic of replication, not succession.
lds.restoration: The LDS Restoration claims new scripture, priesthood keys, and living apostles after total apostasy. This is the strongest restorationist claim and the farthest from Catholic indefectibility.
restorationist.restoration: Restorationism as a family believes primitive Christianity must be rebuilt from the Bible. Catholic Tradition and succession say the Church never needed refounding. The primitive pattern replaces the living Magisterium.
adventist.sabbath: Adventists keep Saturday as the seventh-day Sabbath as a creation and moral obligation. Catholics keep Sunday as the Lord's Day, the weekly memorial of the Resurrection, not a transferred Saturday Sabbath in Adventist terms. Sunday obligation is ecclesiastical and paschal.
lds.sabbath: Latter-day Saints keep Sunday as the Sabbath day of rest and worship in practice. The Word of Wisdom and sacrament meeting structure the day. Theology is less about seventh-day creation law than Adventist teaching.
messianic.sabbath: Messianic believers typically keep Shabbat from Friday sundown to Saturday sundown as Torah faithfulness in Messiah. Catholics do not bind Christians to Saturday rest. The Lord's Day remains Sunday.
protestant.sabbath: Protestants split among Sunday-as-Christian-Sabbath, Lord's Day without strict Sabbatarianism, and seventh-day groups. Catholic Sunday is fulfillment in the Resurrection, with precept to hear Mass. Puritan Sabbath strictness is not Catholic.
seventh_day_adventist.sabbath: Seventh-day Adventists make Saturday Sabbath a mark of true worship and often read Sunday laws as a future mark of apostasy. This polemically targets Catholic Sunday. The Church sees Sunday as apostolic custom confirmed by Tradition, not the mark of the beast.
adventist.soul_sleep: Adventists teach the unconscious state of the dead until resurrection. Catholic doctrine of the immortal soul, particular judgment, heaven, hell, and purgatory is incompatible with soul sleep.
christadelphian.soul_sleep: Christadelphians teach that the dead are asleep or nonexistent until resurrection; there is no immortal soul. This denies the Catholic intermediate state entirely.
jehovahs_witnesses.soul_sleep: Jehovah's Witnesses teach the dead are unconscious; souls do not live on. A limited number go to heaven; most hope for earthly resurrection. Catholic communion of saints and prayers for the dead collapse on this anthropology.
protestant.soul_sleep: Most Protestants hold a conscious intermediate state with Christ or in misery. A minority holds soul sleep. Catholic teaching is the conscious particular judgment.
seventh_day_adventist.soul_sleep: Seventh-day Adventists officially teach that the dead know nothing until Christ returns. Invocation of saints is therefore impossible. This is a defining contrast with Catholic cultus of the saints.
adventist.tithing: Adventists commonly require a tithe for the support of ministry. Catholics teach stewardship and offerings, with tithe as a worthy practice but not the same covenantal system. Obligation to support the Church exists in canon law without a universal ten-percent dogma.
evangelical.tithing: Many Evangelicals preach the tithe as a biblical minimum. Catholics emphasize free, proportionate giving and justice. Tithing talk is more law-like in some Evangelical settings than in contemporary Catholic pastoral practice.
lds.tithing: Latter-day Saints treat an honest tithe as required for temple recommend and standing. It is a revealed law of the Restoration. Catholic giving is obligatory in principle but not a ticket to a temple ordinance.
protestant.tithing: Protestants vary from tithe teaching to free-will offerings. There is no Catholic canonical parallel uniformly applied. Stewardship is the shared word.
anabaptist.head_covering: Many Anabaptist women wear a prayer covering in obedience to 1 Corinthians 11. Catholic chapel veils are a custom, not a universal law since the 1983 Code. Anabaptist covering is identity and ordinance, not optional devotion.
ortho.head_covering: In many Orthodox churches women cover the head in liturgy. It is custom and piety, comparable to older Catholic practice. It is not a defined dogma.
protestant.head_covering: Most modern Protestants do not require head covering. Where it survives it is a holiness or complementarian sign. Catholics no longer bind it by law.
anabaptist.pacifism: Anabaptists classically refuse war and violence (nonresistance). Catholic just-war teaching allows lethal force under strict conditions. The Anabaptist reading of the Sermon on the Mount is more absolute.
mennonite.pacifism: Mennonites maintain a peace witness against participation in war. Catholics may honor conscientious objection but do not make pacifism the only licit stance. The difference is just war versus nonresistance.
protestant.pacifism: Protestants include both just-war majorities and pacifist minorities. There is no single position. Catholic tradition is predominantly just-war with a pacifist strand of witness.
quaker.pacifism: Friends hold a peace testimony refusing war. This is closer to Anabaptist nonresistance than to Catholic just war. Discernment in the Spirit replaces just-war casuistry.
anabaptist.oaths: Anabaptists often refuse judicial oaths, citing the Sermon on the Mount. Catholics permit oaths in justice. The Anabaptist yea and nay is a holiness discipline.
protestant.oaths: Most Protestants allow oaths. Quakers and some Anabaptists do not. Catholic moral theology allows oaths when necessary and truthful.
quaker.oaths: Quakers refuse oaths and offer affirmations. They see oaths as implying a double standard of truth. Catholics do not treat oaths as inherently evil.
anglican.confession: Anglicans provide auricular confession as optional. Catholics require Confession of mortal sins. Anglican priesthood is not recognized as valid by Rome, which affects the Catholic view of the rite's sacramentality.
ortho.confession: Orthodox Confession is a Mystery, usually face to face with a spiritual father. It is the analogue of Penance. There is no exact Latin taxonomy of mortal and venial as the structure of what must be confessed, though serious sins are confessed.
protestant.confession: Most Protestants confess sins directly to God, sometimes to one another, without a priestly absolution in persona Christi. Catholic sacramental absolution is the dividing line. Confession often means a conversion narrative, not the sacrament.
anglican.confirmation: Anglican Confirmation is a rite of mature commitment, often required before communion in older practice. Catholics see Confirmation as a sacrament conferring the Spirit, ordinarily by a bishop. Validity of Anglican Confirmation follows the Catholic judgment on Anglican orders.
lutheran.confirmation: Lutheran confirmation is typically catechetical, not a third sacrament of the same rank as Baptism and Eucharist. Catholics distinguish the sacrament of Confirmation from a graduation rite. Some Lutheran language of strengthening by the Spirit is close pastorally.
oriental_ortho.confirmation: Oriental Orthodox chrismate immediately after Baptism, as Eastern Catholics do. This is the same mystery Catholics call Confirmation. The minister and timing follow Eastern custom.
ortho.confirmation: Orthodox Chrismation is Confirmation: seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit, given with Baptism even to infants. Catholics recognize it. Latin separation of Confirmation to a later age is a disciplinary difference.
protestant.confirmation: In many Protestant bodies confirmation is a class and public profession, not a sacrament. It does not confer character as Catholic Confirmation does.
anglican.ecumenical_councils: Anglicans generally honor the first four or seven councils as a standard of orthodoxy, with Scripture remaining supreme. Catholics recognize twenty-one ecumenical councils. Later councils defining papal dogma are not received as binding by Anglicans.
church_of_the_east.ecumenical_councils: The Church of the East classically received Nicaea and Constantinople and had a complex relation to Ephesus. Christological formulas of two qnome differ from Chalcedonian Catholic wording. They do not receive the later Catholic list of councils.
oriental_ortho.ecumenical_councils: Oriental Orthodox receive three councils (Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus) and reject Chalcedon as they understand it. Catholics receive Chalcedon as ecumenical. Modern dialogues have narrowed the perceived gap on Christ's natures.
ortho.ecumenical_councils: Eastern Orthodox receive seven ecumenical councils and deny that later Latin councils are ecumenical. Catholics count those later councils as binding. Shared ground is the first seven.
protestant.ecumenical_councils: Protestants may respect early councils insofar as they agree with Scripture. They are not an independent infallible Magisterium. Nicaea and Chalcedon are often accepted in practice; Trent and Vatican I are not.
anglican.holy_orders: Anglicans claim the threefold ministry of bishop, priest, and deacon. Apostolicae curae judged the orders invalid. Anglicans themselves treat Orders as a sacrament in a way many Protestants do not.
ortho.holy_orders: Orthodox Holy Orders are a Mystery; Catholics recognize Orthodox ordination as valid. Married parish priests are ordinary in Orthodoxy. The doctrine of character and priesthood is closely analogous.
protestant.holy_orders: Most Protestants have ordination as authorization to ministry, not a sacrament imprinting an indelible character. The Catholic sacrificial priesthood is rejected or sharply revised.
anglican.liturgy: Anglican worship is classically the Book of Common Prayer: structured, lectionary-based, sacramental. Catholics will find it familiar in shape, though Eucharistic theology varies across parties. It is not the Roman Missal.
lutheran.liturgy: Lutherans keep a Divine Service close to the Western Mass in outline, with justification by faith coloring the theology of the supper. Catholic Mass is a propitiatory sacrifice; Lutheran liturgy is typically not described that way.
oriental_ortho.liturgy: Oriental Orthodox celebrate ancient Divine Liturgies or Holy Qurbana. Catholics of corresponding rites share much of this heritage. It is fully sacramental worship, not a Protestant service of the word only.
ortho.liturgy: The Orthodox Divine Liturgy is the Eucharistic sacrifice and communion of the Church. Catholics recognize it as a true Mass in essence. The Byzantine rite is the most familiar Eastern analogue to Latin Mass.
protestant.liturgy: Protestant order of worship ranges from set liturgy to free Evangelical services. Word and preaching often overshadow sacrament. Catholic liturgy is first the Mass as sacrifice and paschal banquet.
quaker.liturgy: Quakers gather in waiting worship, often silence, until the Spirit prompts speech. There is no Eucharist, no priest, no set Mass. This is the far opposite of Catholic sacramental liturgy.
anglican.matrimony: Anglicans treat marriage as a covenant and, in many formularies, as having a sacramental character, while allowing divorce and remarriage more readily than Rome. Catholics hold marriage between the baptized as a sacrament and intrinsically indissoluble. Annulment is not Anglican divorce.
lds.matrimony: Temple sealing makes marriage for time and eternity if the couple is faithful. Catholic marriage ends at death and does not extend as a sealed eternal companionship in the LDS sense. Civil LDS marriages outside the temple are not the highest form.
ortho.matrimony: Orthodox crowning is the Mystery of Marriage. Economia may allow divorce and a second or third marriage with a penitential rite. Catholics do not dissolve a ratified consummated sacramental marriage; Orthodox economia is the practical contrast.
protestant.matrimony: Protestants generally deny that marriage is a sacrament in the Catholic sevenfold list, while still blessing it in church. Divorce discipline varies. Indissolubility is weaker than Catholic dogma.
anglican.papal_infallibility: Anglicans reject papal infallibility as defined in 1870. Authority is dispersed among Scripture, tradition, reason, and synods. Ex cathedra definitions are not binding on them.
old_catholic.papal_infallibility: Old Catholics separated after Vatican I precisely to reject papal infallibility. They may retain much Catholic liturgy while denying the dogma. For Rome they are not in full communion.
ortho.papal_infallibility: Orthodox reject papal infallibility and locate indefectibility in the Church as a whole, expressed in council and consensus. They may speak of the infallibility of the Church, not of the bishop of Rome as a person in office.
protestant.papal_infallibility: Protestants reject papal infallibility as unbiblical and historically unwarranted. Scripture alone, or Scripture plus lesser authorities, replaces a living infallible office.
anglican.papal_primacy: Anglicans may grant the bishop of Rome a historic primacy of honor or a reformed universal ministry, but not ordinary universal jurisdiction. Catholic Vatican I primacy is not accepted.
old_catholic.papal_primacy: Old Catholics reject Vatican I jurisdiction and infallibility while sometimes allowing a limited primacy of honor. They broke over the definition of papal dogmas. Communion with Utrecht is not communion with Rome.
oriental_ortho.papal_primacy: Oriental Orthodox honor ancient Roman prestige but do not accept universal jurisdiction. Their catholicos-patriarchs govern their churches. Dialogue continues; the Catholic claim remains the obstacle.
ortho.papal_primacy: Orthodox may grant a primacy of honor to Rome among the ancient patriarchates, not supremacy of jurisdiction over other bishops. First among equals is their phrase. Catholic ordinary, immediate, universal jurisdiction is denied.
protestant.papal_primacy: Protestants generally see the papacy as a historical development without divine institution as Catholics define it. Some speak harshly of the papal office; others are irenic but still non-papal.
anglican.perpetual_virginity: Some Anglicans, especially Anglo-Catholics, accept Mary's perpetual virginity; many Evangelicals in Anglicanism do not. The brothers of Jesus are often read as true siblings in Protestant-leaning circles. Catholic dogma is not required.
lutheran.perpetual_virginity: Luther and many early Lutherans affirmed Mary ever-virgin. Later Lutheranism often let the doctrine recede. It is not a Lutheran shibboleth as it is a Catholic dogma.
ortho.perpetual_virginity: Orthodox firmly teach that Mary is ever-virgin. This agrees with Catholic dogma. The brothers of the Lord are relatives, not sons of Mary.
protestant.perpetual_virginity: Many Protestants hold that Mary had other children with Joseph. Perpetual virginity is seen as extra-biblical. Catholic and Orthodox consensus is not decisive for them.
reformed.perpetual_virginity: Reformed theology commonly reads the brothers of the Lord as Mary's children and does not require perpetual virginity. Calvin sometimes spoke cautiously; later Reformed piety did not feature the dogma.
anglican.polity: Anglicans are episcopal: bishops, priests, deacons, with synods. This looks Catholic in structure. Royal or parliamentary involvement in some provinces and the lack of papal communion distinguish it.
baptist.polity: Baptists are congregational: the local church is autonomous under Christ. Catholic hierarchical communion is the opposite model. Associations exist without binding a bishop over the congregation.
congregational.polity: Congregationalists vest authority in the gathered local church. Elders or ministers serve by consent. There is no diocesan bishop in the Catholic sense.
ortho.polity: Orthodox polity is conciliar and patriarchal, with autocephalous churches. Synodality is stronger than a single universal ordinary. Catholics see a lack of a visible universal primate with jurisdiction.
presbyterian.polity: Presbyterians govern by graded courts of elders: session, presbytery, general assembly. This is neither papal nor purely congregational. Holy Orders as sacrifice are absent.
protestant.polity: Protestant government is a spectrum: episcopal, presbyterian, congregational. Polity is often treated as secondary to the gospel. Catholic polity is doctrinal, not merely practical.
anglican.purgatory: Classical Anglicanism rejected purgatory as Rome taught it (Article XXII), though some Anglicans now speak of an intermediate purification. Catholics define purgatory as purification of the saved. Anglican intermediate state may be a milder, undefined analogue.
ortho.purgatory: Orthodox reject the Latin school system of purgatorial fire and quantified satisfaction, yet pray for the dead and allow a process of growth after death. Catholics see a material agreement on prayer for the departed; Orthodox refuse the word and the medieval imagery.
protestant.purgatory: Most Protestants deny purgatory as unbiblical and as undermining the sufficiency of the Cross. The saved go to Christ's presence; the lost to punishment. Suffrages for the dead are dropped.
anglican.rosary: Some Anglicans use an Anglican rosary or even the Dominican rosary as devotion. It is optional piety, not a mark of ecclesial identity. Catholic indulgenced Dominican Rosary is a specific meditation on the mysteries with Mary.
ortho.rosary: Orthodox use the prayer rope for the Jesus Prayer more than the Marian rosary. The analogue is repetitive contemplative prayer, not the same mystery structure. Marian akathists fill some of the same devotional space.
anglican.sign_of_the_cross: Many Anglicans sign themselves, especially Anglo-Catholics. It is permitted variety. For Catholics it is an ordinary sacramental of the Latin and Eastern faithful.
lutheran.sign_of_the_cross: Luther retained the sign of the cross, and some Lutherans use it. It is not universal in Protestantism. Catholics use it constantly as baptismal remembrance.
oriental_ortho.sign_of_the_cross: Oriental Orthodox sign the cross, often in a distinctive direction or finger position. The meaning—belonging to the Crucified—is the same family of practice as Catholics and Eastern Orthodox.
ortho.sign_of_the_cross: Orthodox sign from right to left with particular fingers confessing the Trinity and two natures. Catholics of the Latin rite sign left to right. The sacramental is shared; the choreography differs.
anglican.sola_scriptura: Anglicans classically hold Scripture as the supreme authority, with tradition and reason as helpers. This is softer than some Reformed sola scriptura. Catholics hold Scripture and Tradition as one deposit interpreted by the Magisterium.
lutheran.sola_scriptura: Lutherans teach that Scripture is the only rule of faith that can bind the conscience, while honoring creeds and confessions as witnesses. Catholic Magisterium is not a parallel norm. The Book of Concord functions as a subordinate standard.
ortho.sola_scriptura: Orthodox reject sola scriptura and hold Scripture within Holy Tradition. This is structurally closer to Catholics than to Protestants. They do not, however, accept a papal Magisterium as the living voice of that Tradition.
protestant.sola_scriptura: Sola scriptura is the Protestant formal principle: Scripture alone is the final infallible authority. Catholics answer with Scripture, Tradition, and Magisterium. Alone is the conflict word.
reformed.sola_scriptura: Reformed churches articulate sola scriptura with a high view of confessions as accurate summaries, not as rivals to the Bible. Private interpretation is still checked by the analogy of faith and church courts. It remains opposed to a teaching office that claims infallibility.
anglican.theotokos: Anglo-Catholics gladly say Theotokos or Mother of God; Evangelical Anglicans may prefer mother of Jesus to avoid Marian devotion. The Council of Ephesus title is Catholic dogma about Christ. Anglican usage tracks churchmanship.
church_of_the_east.theotokos: The Church of the East historically preferred Christotokos against what they feared as confusion of natures. Modern statements have narrowed the gap with Catholic Theotokos language. The old polemical contrast was about protecting the distinction of natures.
oriental_ortho.theotokos: Oriental Orthodox confess Mary as Theotokos with great liturgical honor. This agrees with Catholic dogma. Miaphysite Christology still intends the one incarnate Lord whom Mary bore.
ortho.theotokos: Theotokos is dogmatic and liturgical center for Orthodox as for Catholics. The title defends the Incarnation. Veneration of the Panagia is intense; the dogmatic core matches Ephesus.
protestant.theotokos: Many Protestants avoid Mother of God as sounding as if Mary originated the divinity. Catholics explain it as Mother of the divine Person according to the flesh. Protestant reserve is often about piety more than the metaphysics of Ephesus.
anglican.tradition: Anglicans value tradition as a guide subordinate to Scripture. Catholic Sacred Tradition is a mode of transmission of the same divine revelation, not only custom. Anglican tradition can be reformed by Scripture in a way Catholic dogma cannot be repealed.
oriental_ortho.tradition: Oriental Orthodox live by Holy Tradition: liturgy, fathers, canons. This is close to Catholic sense of Tradition as living transmission. The content diverges where councils after Ephesus are not shared.
ortho.tradition: Holy Tradition is the life of the Spirit in the Church, including Scripture. Catholics agree that Tradition is not a set of extras beside the Bible. Orthodox locate its authentic voice in Orthodox liturgy and fathers, not in the pope.
protestant.tradition: Protestants may honor tradition as fallible wisdom. It cannot bind against Scripture. Catholic Sacred Tradition is a stronger claim—divine revelation handed on.
assyrian.natures_of_christ: The Assyrian Church of the East is dyophysite in a distinctive idiom of two natures and two qnome in one personhood of Christ. Catholics judge that modern agreed statements show the intent was not Nestorian heresy as popularly charged. Vocabulary still does not match Chalcedonian hypostatic union word for word.
church_of_the_east.natures_of_christ: The Church of the East insists on a strict distinction of divinity and humanity to protect both. Catholics use hypostatic union: one Person, two natures. Dialogue has claimed the faith is the same expressed differently.
jehovahs_witnesses.natures_of_christ: Jehovah's Witnesses teach that Jesus is the first created being, not consubstantial God incarnate. This is not two natures in one divine Person but a creature who lived as a man. Catholic Incarnation and Trinity are denied.
lds.natures_of_christ: Latter-day Saints teach Jesus as the divine Son, Jehovah of the Old Testament, who took a mortal body. Father and Son are distinct beings of flesh and glory. This is not Chalcedonian two natures in one consubstantial Son.
oneness_pentecostal.natures_of_christ: Oneness theology says God was manifest in flesh: Jesus is the Father in his deity and the Son in his humanity. Catholics insist the Son is a distinct Person who assumes a human nature. Oneness manifestation is not the hypostatic union of the second Person.
oriental_ortho.natures_of_christ: Oriental Orthodox are miaphysite: one incarnate nature of the Word, divinity and humanity united without separation. They reject being called Monophysite in the Eutychian sense. Catholics believe Chalcedon's two natures states the same mystery in different words, as recent declarations often say.
ortho.natures_of_christ: Orthodox are Chalcedonian: one Person, two natures, without confusion or change. This is Catholic Christology. Disputes with Rome are not here.
protestant.natures_of_christ: Classical Protestants confess Chalcedon: fully God and fully man. Liberal Protestantism may reduce Christ to a merely human teacher. Confessional Protestant Christology is the Catholic doctrine of the two natures without the later Marian and ecclesial developments.
lds.christian_status: Latter-day Saints insist they are Christian because they worship Jesus Christ as Son of God and Savior. Many Catholics and other Christians answer that Nicene Trinity and the sufficiency of the biblical canon are part of what Christian has meant. The debate is over the definition of the name, not over whether LDS use Jesus' name.
protestant.communion: Protestants call it the Lord's Supper or Holy Communion. The spectrum runs from Lutheran Real Presence to Reformed spiritual presence to memorialism. None officially teach transubstantiation; Catholic Mass as sacrifice is generally rejected.
baptist.deacons: Baptist deacons are local church officers for service and often governance, usually not clergy in a sacramental sense. Catholic deacons are in Holy Orders. The name is shared; the sacrament is not.
lds.deacons: LDS deacons are typically twelve-year-old boys in the Aaronic priesthood who pass the sacrament. This does not map onto the Catholic diaconate as a grade of Holy Orders. Age and function are wholly different.
ortho.deacons: Orthodox deacons are clergy who serve the Liturgy and the bishop, as Catholic deacons do. They do not ordinarily preside at the Eucharist. The order is recognizably the same mystery.
protestant.deacons: Protestant deacons range from liturgical assistants to board members. Catholic theology of the diaconate as a sacrament is usually absent.
baptist.elders: Many Baptists now have a plurality of elders or pastors; others have a single pastor plus deacons. Elder means pastoral overseer, not a sacramental priest. Catholic presbyter is a priest who offers the Mass.
lds.elders: Elder is an office in the Melchizedek priesthood, often held by young missionaries and adult men. It is not the Catholic presbyterate. The title is organizational and priestly in an LDS key sense.
presbyterian.elders: Presbyterians distinguish teaching elders (ministers) and ruling elders (lay governors). Together they form the session. This presbyter is not a sacrificing priest.
protestant.elders: Elder language across Protestantism means pastoral or governing office from the New Testament. Catholic priests are elders in etymology but priests in function.
reformed.elders: Reformed church order is rule by elders. Christ governs his church through this office. It is a deliberate alternative to episcopal and papal government.
baptist.local_church: The local congregation is the primary visible church, autonomous under Christ. Catholic parish is a portion of the diocese, not a sovereign church. Baptist church often means the local assembly first.
churches_of_christ.local_church: Each congregation is independent, with elders when possible, no denominational headquarters. Catholic communion of churches under bishops and the pope is rejected as extra-biblical.
protestant.local_church: Protestants emphasize the congregation gathered around Word and sacrament or ordinance. Catholic ecclesiology starts from the universal Church and the diocese. Both care about parish life; the ontology differs.
baptist.mode_of_baptism: Immersion is often treated as the only valid or at least the only proper mode. Catholics hold pouring or immersion valid; mode does not make the sacrament. Baptist insistence is a mark of identity.
oneness_pentecostal.mode_of_baptism: Immersion in Jesus' name is required. Mode and formula together condition validity for them. Catholic validity needs true matter, Trinitarian form, and intention, not Jesus-name-only wording.
ortho.mode_of_baptism: Triple immersion is the Orthodox norm and theological sign of burial with Christ. Catholics allow infusion. Orthodox sometimes question non-immersion baptisms; Catholic practice is broader in mode.
protestant.mode_of_baptism: Protestants disagree: immersion, pouring, or sprinkling. Mode is often secondary to the meaning. Catholic law prefers but does not exclusively require immersion.
baptist.ordination: Baptist ordination is the church's recognition of a call, usually by other pastors. It does not confer indelible priestly character. A Baptist minister is not a Catholic priest.
lds.ordination: Ordination is by laying on of hands by those holding priesthood keys, beginning often in boyhood for Aaronic offices. Catholic ordination is a sacrament reserved to men called to Holy Orders, not a general male progression of offices.
ortho.ordination: Orthodox cheirotonia by a bishop makes deacons, priests, and bishops. Catholics recognize these orders. Married men may be ordained priests; bishops are chosen from the celibate, usually monastic, clergy.
protestant.ordination: Protestant ordination authorizes Word-and-sacrament or Word-and-ordinance ministry. It is not Catholic Holy Orders. Women may be ordained in many bodies, unlike Catholic practice.
baptist.ordination_of_women: Baptists are split: some conventions ordain women as pastors; others forbid it from Pauline texts. Catholics hold the Church has no authority to ordain women to the priesthood. The Baptist debate is congregational and exegetical, not a claim about sacrament as character.
lds.ordination_of_women: LDS priesthood offices are conferred on men; women have authority in auxiliaries and exercise some temple roles without being ordained to priesthood offices as men are. Catholic reservation of Holy Orders to men is a different structure, but both are male in the priestly office.
methodist.ordination_of_women: Most large Methodist bodies ordain women as elders and bishops. Catholics judge such ordination invalid for priestly orders. Methodism treats call and fruit as decisive, not male-only apostolic example as a permanent bar.
ortho.ordination_of_women: Orthodox do not ordain women as priests or bishops. Some discuss a restored female diaconate. The practical conclusion matches Catholic priesthood reservation; the canonical reasoning is their own tradition.
protestant.ordination_of_women: Protestantism is divided. Where women are ordained, the theology of Orders as a sacrificing priesthood is usually already rejected. Catholic teaching in Ordinatio sacerdotalis is not accepted.
baptist.perseverance: Many Baptists teach eternal security: once truly saved, always saved. Catholics teach that mortal sin can lose sanctifying grace and that final perseverance is a gift. Baptist security is stronger than Catholic hope and weaker on the possibility of falling.
evangelical.perseverance: Evangelicals often teach once saved, always saved, or else a Wesleyan possibility of falling. Catholic mortal sin as loss of justification is denied by the always-saved camp.
lds.perseverance: Latter-day Saints insist one must endure to the end for exaltation. That is closer to Catholic warning against presumption than to eternal security. Grace and ordinances remain required along the path.
methodist.perseverance: Methodists teach that a Christian may fall from grace by willful sin. This is nearer Catholic possibility of losing justification than Reformed perseverance of the saints. Assurance is not an unconditional guarantee.
reformed.perseverance: Perseverance of the saints: those truly elect will be kept and will not finally fall. Catholics allow real apostasy of the justified. Reformed perseverance is tied to unconditional election, not to Catholic synergy and sacramental restoration after a fall.
baptist.priesthood_of_believers: Soul competency and the priesthood of all believers mean each person stands before God without a mediating priestly caste. Catholics teach a common priesthood of the baptized and a distinct ministerial priesthood. Baptists collapse the second into the first.
lds.priesthood_of_believers: LDS men may hold priesthood offices; it is not the Protestant every-believer-is-his-own-priest in the same way, nor the Catholic common-plus-ministerial pair. Authority is hierarchical by keys.
protestant.priesthood_of_believers: The Reformation doctrine that all the baptized share priestly access to God rejects a sacrificing ministerial priesthood as Catholics define it. Pastors are ministers of the Word, not priests at an altar of propitiation.
christian_science.incarnation: Christian Science distinguishes the eternal Christ as divine idea from the man Jesus. This is not the Word assuming a human nature. Matter and bodily suffering are metaphysically downplayed; Catholic flesh of the Incarnation is central and real.
christian_science.scripture: Christian Science reads the Bible through Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures by Mary Baker Eddy. That second book functions as an interpretive authority Catholics would compare to an extra-canonical magisterial text—and reject as such.
christadelphian.preexistence_of_christ: Christadelphians deny that Christ personally preexisted his conception. He came into being in the womb of Mary. Catholics confess the eternal Son, begotten before all ages, who became flesh.
christadelphian.trinity: Christadelphians are unitarian in a biblical-unitarian sense: God is one Father; Jesus is the human Son. The Catholic Trinity is rejected as post-biblical. There is no consubstantial Son or Spirit as Person.
iglesia_ni_cristo.one_true_church: Iglesia ni Cristo claims to be the true Church of Christ restored in the last days. Catholics hold the Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church. Both make exclusive claims; they cannot both be true as stated.
iglesia_ni_cristo.trinity: Iglesia ni Cristo teaches that the Father alone is God; Jesus is the Son but not God. This is a denial of Nicaea. Catholic baptismal faith in three Persons is incompatible.
iglesia_ni_cristo.true_church_claim: Their true-church claim is restorationist and exclusive. Catholic subsistence claim is historical and apostolic. Dialogue language of separated brethren is not how INC describes Catholics.
jehovahs_witnesses.father: Jehovah is the personal name of the Father, the one true God. Catholics say God the Father as first Person of the Trinity, not as the only divine person. Using the name Jehovah as the almost exclusive divine name is a Witness distinctive.
jehovahs_witnesses.heaven: Only 144,000 have a heavenly hope to reign with Christ; most of the faithful look to paradise earth. Catholic heaven is the destiny of all the saints in the beatific vision. The two-class hope is foreign to Catholic eschatology.
jehovahs_witnesses.hell: Witnesses deny hell as eternal torment; Gehenna is annihilation. Hades is the common grave. Catholic hell is eternal separation and punishment.
jehovahs_witnesses.holy_spirit: The holy spirit is God's impersonal active force, not the third Person. Catholic pneumatology presupposes a Person. Witnesses would see Catholic prayer to the Spirit as misguided.
jehovahs_witnesses.name_of_god: Restoring the name Jehovah is essential to true worship. Catholics traditionally pray Lord following Jewish and Septuagint practice and do not treat the Tetragrammaton as a required spoken form in the liturgy.
jehovahs_witnesses.new_creation: The main hope is a restored Paradise Earth under the Kingdom. Catholics hope for new heavens and new earth and the beatific vision, not an earthbound paradise as the ordinary goal of the saints.
jehovahs_witnesses.preexistence_of_chris: Jesus preexisted as the first creation, identified with Michael the archangel. Catholics confess eternal generation, not first creature. Arian-like structure is the historical Catholic name for this pattern.
jehovahs_witnesses.resurrection_of_the_d: Most will be raised to a chance of life on earth; some to heaven as spirit creatures. Catholic resurrection is bodily for all, then judgment to heaven or hell. Witness anthropology has no immortal soul awaiting reunion.
jehovahs_witnesses.trinity: The Trinity is rejected as unbiblical. Jehovah is one person. Catholic dogma of one God in three Persons is the opposite claim.
unitarian.trinity: Unitarian Christians hold that God is one Person, the Father, and that Jesus is Lord in a moral or messianic sense, not consubstantial God. Catholic faith begins with baptism into the Trinity.
oneness_pentecostal.father: Father is a title of the one God in a mode of relationship, not a distinct Person eternally distinct from the Son. Catholics distinguish Persons, not mere titles.
oneness_pentecostal.holy_spirit: The Holy Ghost is the one God in spiritual action and indwelling, not a third Person. Catholic distinction of the Spirit from the Father and the Son is denied. Tongues as evidence is attached to this pneumatology.
oneness_pentecostal.name_of_god: The saving name is Jesus; baptism and prayer invoke that name. Catholics baptize in the threefold name and honor the name of Jesus without collapsing the Trinity into it.
oneness_pentecostal.repentance: Repentance is the first step in a three-part new birth: repent, be baptized in Jesus' name, receive the Holy Ghost with tongues. Catholic repentance is contrition and Confession, with Baptism as the first sacrament, not this three-step Oneness plan.
oneness_pentecostal.tongues: Tongues are the initial evidence of Spirit baptism and thus of the full new-birth experience. Catholics list tongues as a possible charism, not a required sign of having the Spirit.
oneness_pentecostal.trinity: Oneness replaces Trinity with one God who manifests as Father, Son, and Spirit. Catholics call this modalism historically. The baptismal confession is not the same.
oneness_pentecostal.foot_washing: Some Oneness churches keep foot washing as an ordinance with baptism and communion. Catholics know the Holy Thursday mandatum as a sign of service, not a sacrament of initiation.
messianic.name_of_god: Messianic believers often use Hashem, YHVH, or spoken forms like Yahweh and Yeshua to stress Jewish continuity. Catholics use Lord, Father, Jesus, Christ in the liturgy. The reverence overlaps; the Hebraic naming program is distinctive.
community_of_christ.open_canon: Community of Christ keeps an open canon including the Book of Mormon and Doctrine and Covenants in its own recension, while moving toward mainline Protestant conversation partners. Catholics have a closed canon.
community_of_christ.temples: They have temples as centers of peace and learning, not LDS endowment-and-sealing complexes in the same way. Catholic churches and the eschatological temple-body of Christ are the Catholic analogues, not a restored House of the Lord for proxy work.
community_of_christ.mormon_label: Community of Christ formerly used RLDS and has distanced itself from the nickname Mormon. Catholics should not assume every Mormon label fits them. They present as a Christian church with Restoration roots.
lds.canon: Standard works: Bible, Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants, Pearl of Great Price. The canon is open to new revelation. Catholic canon is closed; additional LDS scriptures are not recognized.
lds.continuing_revelation: Living prophets can announce new doctrine and policy as revelation. Catholics hold public revelation ended with the Apostles; private revelation cannot revise dogma. A living prophet is not the Magisterium.
lds.election: Foreordination in a premortal life explains callings; it is not always Calvinist predestination to heaven or hell. Catholic predestination concerns grace and glory without premortal human spirits as LDS teach.
lds.father: Heavenly Father (Elohim) is a distinct exalted being with a glorified body. Catholics confess the Father as unembodied infinite Spirit, first Person, not an exalted man. Heavenly Father is shared piety with different metaphysics.
lds.free_will: Agency is central and premortal. Catholics defend free will against determinism but do not teach a premortal council of spirits. Synergy is a closer Orthodox and Catholic analogue than LDS agency-in-premortality.
lds.gifts_of_the_spirit: Gifts are expected, including prophecy, healing, and tongues, within priesthood order. Catholics also affirm charisms. Discernment for LDS runs through priesthood authority more than through a bishop's charismatic discernment alone.
lds.glorification: Exaltation in the celestial kingdom, including eternal marriage and becoming like God. Catholic glorification is the beatific vision and risen life, not celestial marriage as a condition of highest glory.
lds.grace: Grace is real but often paired with after all we can do, a phrase debated even among Saints. Catholics teach grace as primary and meritorious works as themselves graced. The slogan can sound semi-Pelagian to Catholic ears; LDS intend covenant cooperation.
lds.heaven: Heaven is differentiated into kingdoms of glory. Catholic heaven is one blessed life of seeing God, with degrees of charity, not separate kingdoms.
lds.hell: Hell language includes spirit prison and, for a few, outer darkness. Most are not endlessly tormented. Catholic hell is definitive for those who die in mortal sin unrepentant.
lds.holy_spirit: The Holy Ghost is a spirit personage in the Godhead, distinct from the Father and the Son. Gift of the Holy Ghost follows baptism by laying on of hands. This looks like Confirmation but sits in a non-Nicene Godhead of three beings.
lds.human_nature: Humans are spirit children of Heavenly Parents, combined with mortal bodies. Catholic anthropology: created from nothing, body and spiritual soul, not premortal spirit children. Natural man in the Book of Mormon names fallen opposition to God.
lds.image_of_god: The imago Dei includes that God has a glorified human form and we are his kind. Catholics teach image as reason, will, and capacity for God, not God's having a body. The mapping is analogical versus more literal.
lds.incarnation: Jesus' mortal birth is real; Mary is his mother. Premortal Jehovah descends to take flesh. Catholic eternal Word made flesh is Nicene; LDS premortal Christ is a distinct divine being who becomes embodied.
lds.inspiration: Scripture is inspired, including modern scripture, yet not every word of the Bible is inerrant in LDS official caution as far as it is translated correctly. Catholic inspiration covers the whole canonical text as the Church receives it.
lds.intercession_of_saints: Prayer is addressed to the Father in the name of the Son, not to saints or Mary as intercessors. Catholics ask the saints to pray. LDS reject that cultus as improper.
lds.justification: Justification is being set right, tied to covenant fidelity and ordinances, not forensic imputation alone. Catholic justification is infusion of grace. LDS usage is more covenantal-restorative than Tridentine.
lds.marriage: Eternal marriage is the highest covenant. Catholic marriage is a sacrament unto death. Sealing has no Catholic equivalent.
lds.mary: Mary is honored as the virgin mother of the Son of God, not as Theotokos in defined Catholic dogmas of Immaculate Conception and Assumption. Devotion is modest compared with Catholic hyperdulia.
lds.mormon_label: The Church now prefers Latter-day Saint, not Mormon Church. Mormon remains a common nickname Catholics will hear. Official style avoids Mormon as the name of the Church.
lds.new_creation: The earth will be renewed and receive celestial glory. Catholics also hope for a new heaven and new earth. LDS cosmology includes specific kingdoms and temple imagery Catholics do not use.
lds.offices_of_christ: Christ is Creator, Redeemer, Judge, Elder Brother. Protestant munus triplex may appear in preaching. The titles sit in LDS Godhead and Restoration frames.
lds.one_true_church: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints claims to be the only true and living church with full keys. Catholics claim the Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church. These exclusivist claims collide.
lds.open_canon: Additional scripture and future revelation keep the canon open. Catholic canon is closed. The Book of Mormon is the distinctive extra book Catholics do not receive.
lds.original_sin: LDS reject inherited guilt of Adam's transgression; the Fall is a necessary step. Children are innocent until accountability. Catholic original sin is inherited lack of original holiness, remitted in infant Baptism.
lds.prayer: Prayers are addressed to the Father in the name of Christ, simply and vocally, without set liturgy required in the home. Catholic prayer includes liturgy of the hours, Mass, and devotion to saints.
lds.prayers_for_the_dead: Proxy baptism, confirmation, and sealing for the dead are temple works. Catholics pray for the dead and offer Mass, but do not rebaptize the deceased. The intention—help the dead—rhymes; the rite does not.
lds.preexistence_of_christ: Christ is the firstborn spirit and Jehovah in a premortal world. Catholic preexistence is eternal generation, not firstborn among spirit siblings.
lds.priesthood: Aaronic and Melchizedek priesthoods are restored organizations of authority. Catholic priesthood is participation in Christ's priesthood through Holy Orders and baptism. The two-order LDS system does not map onto bishop-priest-deacon.
lds.priesthood_authority: Keys held by the President of the Church govern all ordinances. Catholic sacred power is given in Orders and governed by communion with the college of bishops and the pope. Both claim unique valid authority; they deny each other's claim.
lds.prophetic_authority: The living prophet, the President, holds all keys and can speak for God to the Church. Catholics have no single officer who issues new public revelation. The pope interprets a closed deposit; the prophet can expand scripture.
lds.repentance: Repentance is a structured process: recognize, confess, forsake, restitution, as part of enduring to the end. Catholic Confession is sacramental absolution. LDS confession of serious sins is to priesthood leaders, not a priest in persona Christi as Catholics understand it.
lds.resurrection_of_christ: Christ's resurrection is bodily and the cause of universal resurrection. Catholics agree on the fact. LDS attach it to Gethsemane-and-Cross atonement and to degrees of risen glory.
lds.resurrection_of_the_dead: All are raised to a kingdom of glory suited to their lives, except sons of perdition. Catholic resurrection precedes judgment to heaven or hell. Near-universal assignment to a glory is more optimistic than Catholic hell.
lds.sacraments: Saving ordinances—baptism, confirmation, priesthood, endowment, sealing—are required and must be done by authority, including for the dead. Catholics have seven sacraments for the living. Endowment and sealing have no Catholic sacrament match.
lds.salvation: Salvation can mean resurrection from death, almost universal, or exaltation, conditional. Catholics use salvation for deliverance from sin and entrance into the vision of God. Always ask which LDS sense is in view; saved is not exalted.
lds.sanctification: Sanctification is becoming holy through covenants, Spirit, and endurance. Catholic sanctifying grace is a share in the divine life infused in the soul. LDS holiness is covenantal and eschatological toward exaltation.
lds.scripture: The Bible is one among four standard works. Catholic Sacred Scripture is the biblical canon alone as book, read in Tradition. Quoting scripture in LDS speech may mean the Book of Mormon.
lds.second_coming: Christ will return, millennial reign will begin, and temple work will flourish. Catholics confess the Parousia and judgment, not an LDS millennial temple program. Shared hope, different timetable details.
lds.sexual_ethics: The law of chastity forbids sexual relations outside marriage between a man and a woman, with temple worthiness consequences. Catholic chastity is similar in content on adultery and homosexual acts. Contraception teaching is not identical; LDS allow contraception more freely than Humanae vitae.
lds.spirit_world: After death, spirits enter paradise or prison and can accept the gospel. Catholic particular judgment sends the soul to heaven, hell, or purgatory. Prison-as-mission-field is the LDS distinctive.
lds.temples: Temples are reserved buildings for endowment, sealing, and work for the dead, distinct from meetinghouses. Catholic parish churches are public worship sites; a Catholic church is not an LDS temple.
