lds.theosis: Exaltation is becoming like Heavenly Father, including glory, intelligence, and eternal posterity. Catholic divinization is participation, not identity of kind as exalted embodied gods. The word theosis is Orthodox; LDS become like God needs that caveat for Catholic ears.
lds.true_church_claim: Only true and living church is an official phrase. Catholic claim is that the Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church. Both are exclusivist in different metaphysical keys.
lds.virgin_birth: LDS affirm that Mary was a virgin and Jesus is the Son of the Father. Speculative older comments about the mechanism are not the same as defined Catholic dogma. The virginal conception is confessed.
evangelical.continuationism: Evangelicals divide over whether sign gifts continue. Some are charismatic; some are cessationist. Catholics hold that charisms continue as the Spirit wills, without requiring tongues as proof.
evangelical.ecumenism: Evangelicals may cooperate across denominations on mission and morals while remaining wary of Rome and of liberal ecumenism. Catholic ecumenism seeks visible unity in faith and sacrament. Evangelical unity is often spiritual and pragmatic.
evangelical.faith_and_works: Evangelicals preach salvation by faith, not works, while expecting works as fruit. Catholics teach faith formed by charity and the necessity of works of love as conditions of remaining in grace. Sola fide is the flashpoint.
evangelical.headship: Complementarian Evangelicals teach male headship in church and home; egalitarians do not. Catholic complementarity affirms equal dignity and reserved priesthood without always using the complementarian system.
evangelical.inerrancy: Many Evangelicals bind themselves to biblical inerrancy in the original autographs. Catholics teach that Scripture teaches without error the truth God wanted for salvation; the word inerrancy appears in Catholic documents with nuances Evangelicals sometimes find too qualified.
evangelical.new_birth: To be born again is the decisive conversion, often dated and remembered. Catholics locate regeneration primarily in Baptism, with ongoing conversion. Evangelical saved language tracks this new-birth moment.
evangelical.salvation: Saved means justified by faith in Christ, usually in a conversion experience, with assurance. Catholic salvation is a process: justification, sanctification, perseverance, glory. Are you saved does not translate cleanly into Catholic pastoral speech.
evangelical.sacred_music: Contemporary worship songs and historic hymns both appear. Catholic sacred music includes chant and has norms for liturgy that Evangelicals do not use. Style is not a sacrament.
evangelical.separated_brethren: Evangelicals may call other Protestants believers and Catholics nominal or unevangelized if they lack a born-again experience. Catholic separated brethren is irenic toward baptized non-Catholics. The Evangelical question is conversion, not valid baptism only.
evangelical.sexual_ethics: Biblical sexual ethics: marriage between man and woman, chastity outside it. Alignment with Catholic moral conclusions is often close on abortion and same-sex acts. Divorce and contraception usually differ from Catholic law.
holiness.sanctification: Entire sanctification is a second work of grace cleansing the heart from inbred sin. Catholic holiness is growth in infused grace, not usually a single second crisis. Perfection language in Holiness circles is stronger and earlier than Catholic spiritual theology typically allows.
methodist.free_will: Methodists teach prevenient grace that restores ability to respond, against Calvinist inability. Catholics also teach that grace enables free response and deny total inability in the Calvinist sense. Cooperation is a shared instinct.
methodist.means_of_grace: Works of piety and mercy—prayer, sacrament, fasting, Scripture, fellowship—are instituted means of grace. Catholics name the sacraments as the primary instituted means. Wesley's list is broader and less ontologically ranked.
methodist.predestination: Conditional election based on foreseen faith, with prevenient grace for all. Catholic doctrine also rejects double predestination to damnation as Calvin taught it.
methodist.sanctification: Going on to perfection is the Methodist distinctive: love filling the heart in this life. Catholic saints speak of perfection as charity; the Methodist second-blessing package is more programmatic.
reformed.continuationism: Many Reformed are cessationist: miraculous sign gifts ceased with the Apostles. Catholics are continuationist about charisms as such. The Reformed concern is the sufficiency of Scripture against new revelation.
reformed.election: Unconditional election of individuals to salvation. Catholic election is real but not taught as unconditional double predestination. The elect in Reformed speech is a defined company.
reformed.free_will: The will is bound in sin until grace regenerates. Catholics teach wounded but real freedom, needing grace. Reformed free agency after regeneration is not Catholic natural-liberty language.
reformed.grace: Sovereign grace that effectually saves the elect. Catholic grace can be resisted in the ordinary account of actual grace. Irresistible grace is a Reformed distinctive.
reformed.hermeneutics: Scripture interprets Scripture; analogy of faith. Catholics add the living Magisterium and the senses of Scripture including the spiritual. Private interpretation is limited by confessions rather than by a pope.
reformed.justification: Forensic declaration, imputed righteousness of Christ, faith alone. Catholic justification is a making righteous by infused grace. This is the classic Reformation divide.
reformed.means_of_grace: Word and sacraments as means the Spirit uses. Catholic sacraments confer grace. Reformed sacraments are means but not ex opere operato in the Catholic sense.
reformed.offices_of_christ: Munus triplex: prophet, priest, and king. Catholics can use the same triad. It organizes Reformed Christology and ministry.
reformed.original_sin: Total corruption and federal headship of Adam. Catholic original sin is deprivation of original justice and concupiscence, not always total in the Reformed sense. Guilt and imputation language is more forensic.
reformed.predestination: Includes election and, in double-predestinarian forms, reprobation. Catholics condemn the idea that God predestines to evil in the same way. The Reformed decree is the hardest edge for Catholic ears.
reformed.real_presence: Spiritual presence of Christ by the Spirit to faith, not bodily in the elements as Catholics teach. No transubstantiation. Calvin's view is neither Lutheran nor Zwinglian.
reformed.total_depravity: Every faculty is tainted; no one can turn to God without regenerating grace. Catholics teach concupiscence and wounded nature, not the destruction of natural goods. Total does not mean as bad as possible even in Reformed textbooks, but it is still stronger than Catholic wording.
reformed.visible_and_invisible_church: The invisible church is the elect; the visible is mixed. Catholics emphasize the visible sacramental Church. Reformed extra ecclesiam is qualified by election beyond visible bounds more freely.
reformed_baptist.continuationism: Reformed Baptists are commonly cessationist and credobaptist. They combine Calvinist soteriology with Baptist ordinances. Catholic charisms and infant baptism are both rejected.
lutheran.means_of_grace: Word and sacrament are vehicles of the Spirit; baptism and the supper actually give what they promise. This is closer to Catholic sacramental realism than most Reformed or Baptist views. They still reject the sacrifice of the Mass and a seven-sacrament system.
lutheran.real_presence: Sacramental union: Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with, and under bread and wine. Catholics teach a change of substance; Lutherans deny transubstantiation but affirm a robust Real Presence.
lutheran.eucharistic_sacrifice: Lutherans reject the Mass as a propitiatory sacrifice offered to God; it is a testament and gift from God plus a sacrifice of praise. Catholic Mass makes present the one sacrifice of Calvary. This is a primary Reformation protest.
eastern_catholic.clerical_celibacy: Eastern Catholic churches, in communion with Rome, ordinarily ordain married men to the presbyterate; bishops are celibate. Latin Catholics often assume universal priestly celibacy; that is a Latin discipline, not a dogma.
ortho.clerical_celibacy: Orthodox parish priests are commonly married if married before ordination; bishops are monks. Catholics of the Latin rite require celibacy for priests. The Orthodox pattern matches Eastern Catholic discipline.
protestant.clerical_celibacy: Protestant clergy marry freely. Celibacy may be a personal gift, not a condition of office. Catholics see celibacy as a discipline protective of undivided service, not as making marriage unclean.
pentecostal.continuationism: Gifts of 1 Corinthians 12 continue and should be expected in the church. Catholics agree charisms continue, with discernment by the Church. Pentecostal practice is more central to identity than in ordinary Catholic parish life.
pentecostal.gifts_of_the_spirit: Nine gifts of 1 Corinthians 12 are catalogued and sought. Catholics have seven gifts of Isaiah 11 in confirmation catechesis plus Pauline charisms. The lists overlap but are organized differently.
pentecostal.holy_spirit: The Spirit is a Person who fills, empowers, and gives tongues. Catholic dogma of the third Person is shared with Trinitarian Pentecostals. The experiential accent is stronger than typical Latin piety.
pentecostal.preaching: Preaching aims at response, often with altar ministry. Catholic homily breaks open the Word in the Mass. Pentecostal preaching is frequently longer and revivalistic.
pentecostal.prophetic_authority: Some recognize living prophets and personal prophecy. Catholics discern private revelation and do not place prophets over bishops. Prophecy is a charism, not a ruling office replacing the Magisterium.
pentecostal.tongues: Tongues as initial evidence in classical Pentecostalism or as a common prayer gift. Catholics allow the gift, not the evidence doctrine. Uninterpreted tongues in the liturgy are restricted by Paul and by Catholic order.
seventh_day_adventist.continuing_revelat: The Spirit of Prophecy in Ellen G. White is a continuing gift to the remnant, subordinate to the Bible in official theory. Catholics would classify her writings as private revelation at best and not binding. In practice they shape Adventist doctrine heavily.
seventh_day_adventist.open_canon: The biblical canon is closed in theory; the Spirit of Prophecy functions as an authoritative interpretive companion. Catholics would see a quasi-open authority. Ellen White is not a seventy-fourth book officially, but she is more than optional reading.
seventh_day_adventist.prophetic_authorit: Ellen White's prophetic gift is a mark of the remnant church. Catholic public prophecy of that institutional kind ended with the Apostles. Comparing her to a living Magisterium is the nearest Catholic analogue—and a rejected one.
new_apostolic.continuing_revelation: Apostles can still bind the church with living teaching. Catholics close public revelation. Sealing by an apostle has no Catholic sacramental counterpart.
new_apostolic.prophetic_authority: The Chief Apostle is the highest spiritual authority. That role is more centralized than most Protestantism and is not Petrine succession as Catholics define it.
churches_of_christ.faith_and_works: Obedient faith includes baptism as the moment sins are washed. Catholics also tie first justification to Baptism. Churches of Christ deny inherited original sin and infant baptism, so the map is only partial.
churches_of_christ.instrumental_music: Many a cappella Churches of Christ exclude instruments from worship as unauthorized. Catholic liturgy uses instruments freely. The argument is restorationist silence of Scripture, not Catholic sacramentality of music.
churches_of_christ.one_true_church: They often claim to be the church of Christ in a non-denominational, New Testament sense, sometimes with sharp exclusivity. Catholic subsistence claim is historical and sacramental.
restorationist.church: The church must match the New Testament pattern in ordinance and name. Catholic Church claims organic continuity, not replication from a text alone. Undenominational Christianity is the restorationist ideal.
restorationist.true_church_claim: The true church is the restored New Testament church. Catholic true-church claim is apostolic succession and Eucharist. Restorationists see Catholic structure as the problem to be restored away.
adventist.foot_washing: The ordinance of humility accompanies the Lord's Supper. Catholics wash feet on Holy Thursday as a sign, not as a coequal ordinance with the Eucharist. Adventist frequency is communion-service related.
anabaptist.foot_washing: Foot washing is kept as an ordinance of humble service in many Anabaptist communities. Catholic mandatum is liturgical and annual in the Latin rite, not a binding membership ordinance.
adventist.liturgical_calendar: Suspicion of traditional feasts that are seen as unbiblical; Sabbath is the great marker. Catholics live the liturgical year as a sacramental pedagogy. Adventist calendar concern is often anti-Sunday and anti-saint-days.
adventist.second_coming: The soon return of Christ is identity-forming. Catholics also pray come, Lord Jesus without setting prophetic charts of the kind Millerite heritage produced. Imminence is Adventist DNA.
ortho.essence_and_energies: God's essence is incommunicable; his uncreated energies are truly God and the means of theosis. Catholics speak of the simple divine essence and created sanctifying grace. Mapping energies onto created grace is exactly what Orthodox deny; this is a real terminological non-map.
oriental_ortho.essence_and_energies: Oriental Orthodox speak of divine nature and operations without always using Palamite technicalities. Catholics should not force the Palamite scheme on them. Participation in divine life is still the goal.
ortho.filioque: The Spirit proceeds from the Father; the Latin Filioque is judged an illicit addition and a threat to the Father's monarchy. Catholics hold that Filioque names the Spirit's proceeding from the Father and the Son as from one principle. This remains a principal doctrinal dispute.
oriental_ortho.filioque: Oriental Orthodox, like the Eastern Orthodox, do not use the Filioque in the Creed. Procession from the Father is confessed. Catholic explanations of Filioque as not positing two sources have not ended the liturgical difference.
protestant.filioque: Western Protestants generally keep the Filioque as part of the received Latin Creed. They rarely treat it as a live controversy. Catholics and Protestants here share a Western text Orthodox reject.
ortho.icons: Icons are a dogmatic consequence of the Incarnation: the prototype is honored in the image. Catholics agree on venerating images. Orthodox often prefer two-dimensional icons to statues; the theology of veneration is shared against iconoclasm.
oriental_ortho.icons: Oriental Orthodox use icons richly. The theology is incarnational, as with Catholics and Byzantines. Local styles differ; the anti-iconoclast conviction is shared.
protestant.icons: Many Protestants fear images as idolatry. Catholics distinguish veneration from worship of God. Reformed spaces are often bare; Lutheran and Anglican spaces may have art.
reformed.icons: Reformed worship classically excludes images of God and often of the saints from the sanctuary as violations of the second commandment. Catholic sacred images are not, for them, legitimate teaching aids if they become foci of devotion.
ortho.veneration: Proskynesis to icons, relics, and saints is honor, not latreia, which is due to God alone. Catholics use dulia, hyperdulia, latria for the same distinction. The mapping is very close.
protestant.veneration: Protestants often call Catholic veneration worship of saints and reject it. They collapse dulia into latria. Communion of saints for them is fellowship, not invocation.
ortho.jesus_prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner—prayed with the prayer rope toward prayer of the heart. Catholics know the prayer and use it; it is not as central as the Rosary in Latin piety.
oriental_ortho.jesus_prayer: The same Jesus Prayer tradition exists in Oriental monasticism. Catholic readers may treat it as shared Eastern heritage. It is not a sacrament but a way of prayer.
ortho.mary: Mary is Theotokos, ever-virgin, most holy, first among the saints. Defined Latin dogmas of 1854 and 1950 are not Orthodox dogmas, though Dormition and holiness are believed. Hyperdulia is matched in practice if not in Thomas's vocabulary.
oriental_ortho.mary: Intense liturgical honor to the Mother of God. Dogmatic Latin additions are not their vehicle. Shared is more than Protestant honor, less juridically defined than Catholic Marian dogmas.
protestant.mary: Mary is the blessed mother of Jesus, model disciple, not mediatrix of all graces or object of defined privileges. Catholic Marian dogmas and devotion are a major Protestant objection. Honor without invocation is the usual stance.
ortho.immaculate_conception: Orthodox teach Mary's all-holiness but generally reject the Immaculate Conception as framed against Augustinian original sin. They do not need a privilege that exempts her from a guilt they describe differently. Catholics define her preservation from original sin from conception.
protestant.immaculate_conception: Rejected as unbiblical and as making Mary unlike other children of Adam. Catholic dogma is a late definition for them. Virgin birth is not the same doctrine.
ortho.relics: Holy relics are venerated as bearers of grace from the saint's union with God. Catholics agree. The theology is incarnational and sacramental in tone.
protestant.relics: Relics are usually dismissed as superstition. Catholic first-class relics at altars have no Protestant parallel. The concern is idolatry and fraud.
ortho.prayers_for_the_dead: The Church prays for the departed as an act of love; God is not bound by death. Catholics agree and add purgatory as explanation. Orthodox refuse some Latin explanations while keeping the practice.
oriental_ortho.prayers_for_the_dead: Prayers and liturgies for the departed are standard. This matches Catholic suffrages more than Protestant silence. The word purgatory is still not theirs.
protestant.prayers_for_the_dead: Generally rejected as useless or as implying purgatory. The dead in Christ need no help; the lost cannot be helped. Catholic Masses for the dead are a Reformation target.
ortho.canonization_of_saints: Saints are glorified by recognition of existing holiness and popular-liturgical reception, not a papal legal process. Catholics have a formal cause and papal canonization. The outcome—public cult—is similar.
protestant.canonization_of_saints: All believers are saints; there is no canonized list for public veneration. Catholic canonization is seen as extra-biblical. Heroes of faith may be admired without cult.
ortho.heaven: Heaven is communion with God, theosis fulfilled, paradise. Catholic beatific vision is a more Scholastic description of the same hope. Energies versus essence colors how seeing God is phrased.
protestant.heaven: Heaven is being with Christ, the new creation. Beatific vision language is less common. The hope overlaps Catholic eschatology minus purgatory and usually minus theosis vocabulary.
ortho.hell: Hell is real and eternal; often described as the experience of divine love as torment for those who hate it. Catholic teaching includes the pain of loss and of sense. Orthodox resist overly juridical pictures but do not teach annihilation as dogma.
protestant.hell: Classically eternal conscious torment; some now hold annihilation or hope for universalism. Catholic hell is defined as eternal. Protestant variety is wider today than the Catholic dogma.
ortho.resurrection_of_christ: Pascha is the feast of feasts; the Resurrection is the center of the gospel. Catholics agree. The liturgical intensity of Orthodox Pascha is distinctive; the dogma is shared.
protestant.resurrection_of_christ: The empty tomb and risen Lord are essential to orthodox Protestant faith. Liberal denials exist. Shared with Catholics as Creed article.
ortho.resurrection_of_the_dead: The dead will rise bodily. Catholics agree. Hymnography stresses the general resurrection at the Last Day.
protestant.resurrection_of_the_dead: Bodily resurrection is confessed in the Creed many Protestants keep. Some popular piety imagines only souls in heaven. Catholic dogma insists on the body.
ortho.second_coming: The Parousia will be visible and glorious. Catholics agree. Apocalyptic speculation is often more restrained than in Evangelical charts.
protestant.second_coming: The return of Christ is expected; details fragment. Catholic Parousia is one coming in glory. Shared core, disputed timetable.
ortho.new_creation: The cosmos will be transfigured. Catholics speak of new heavens and new earth. Theosis extends toward the whole creation in Orthodox emphasis.
protestant.new_creation: New heavens and new earth from 2 Peter and Revelation. Often less metaphysically developed than Catholic or Orthodox cosmic liturgy. The hope is shared.
ortho.grace: Grace is often identified with uncreated energies, God himself in action. Catholic sanctifying grace is a created habit in the soul. This is a technical non-map even when both say salvation is by grace.
protestant.grace: Unmerited favor, the free gift that saves. Catholic grace includes favor and a real transformation of the soul. Protestant ears hear grace as forensic and relational first.
ortho.justification: Being made righteous in a process of healing, not a single forensic declaration only. Catholics also teach a making righteous. Forensic-only language is the Protestant contrast both Catholics and Orthodox resist.
protestant.justification: Declared righteous by faith on the ground of Christ's righteousness. The article by which the Church stands or falls, for Lutherans. Catholic infusion versus Protestant imputation is the textbook contrast.
ortho.sanctification: The whole Christian life of purification, illumination, theosis. Catholics distinguish justification and sanctification more neatly in the manuals. Orthodox often keep them in one movement of grace.
protestant.sanctification: The process of being made holy after justification. Holiness movements intensify it. Catholic sanctifying grace already is holiness begun at justification.
ortho.faith_and_works: Synergy: God works, man cooperates. Catholics teach cooperating grace. Protestant sola fide is the position both reject as insufficiently synergistic.
protestant.faith_and_works: Works justify before men and prove faith, but do not cause justification. Catholics say works flowing from grace truly merit increase of grace and eternal life. James 2 is read differently.
ortho.predestination: God foreknows and predestines without destroying freedom; double predestination is rejected. Catholic teaching is compatible in outline. Palamite and patristic frames replace Thomist ones.
protestant.predestination: Ranges from Calvinist to Arminian to avoidance of the topic. Catholic doctrine sits between Calvinist double decree and pure Pelagianism. Always ask which Protestant.
ortho.election: The elect are those who freely cooperate with foreknown grace. Reformed unconditional election is too strong. Catholic election language can be used carefully.
protestant.election: Depends on the sub-tradition. Evangelical usage may simply mean the saved. Reformed usage is technical.
ortho.repentance: Metanoia is a lifelong change of mind and heart, concentrated in Confession. Catholic contrition plus Confession is the analogue. Tears and ascesis receive more hagiographic emphasis.
protestant.repentance: Turning from sin to God, often as the first act of conversion. Catholic repentance after baptism is sacramental for mortal sin. Protestant repentance is usually directly to God.
ortho.original_sin: Ancestral sin: mortality and corruption inherited, not Augustinian imputed guilt in the same way. Catholic original sin includes inherited guilt as Trent used the word. Infants need Baptism for life in the Church; Orthodox baptize them without the same guilt theory.
oriental_ortho.original_sin: Similar ancestral-sin emphasis. Shared practice of infant baptism. Latin guilt language is the mismatch.
protestant.original_sin: Generally Augustinian in the magisterial Reformation: inherited guilt and corruption. This is closer to Catholic Trent than to modern Orthodox wording. Baptists still affirm a fallen nature while delaying baptism.
ortho.human_nature: Image and likeness: image remains, likeness is to be restored in theosis. Catholic image and likeness can be used that way. Nature is wounded, not annihilated.
protestant.human_nature: Fallen nature, sometimes total depravity. Catholic wounded nature is the mediating description. Language of sinful nature is common Evangelical speech.
ortho.image_of_god: Image and likeness as above. Icons of Christ imply the image can be depicted. Catholic imago Dei includes dominion and reason; Orthodox add the iconographic implication.
protestant.image_of_god: Imago Dei as reason, relation, or original righteousness lost or marred. Less iconographic consequence. Shared biblical term.
ortho.free_will: Synergy requires real freedom. Calvinist bondage is rejected. Catholic free will after grace is a cousin concept.
protestant.free_will: The great split: bondage versus prevenient grace. Catholic teaching affirms freedom enabled by grace. Do not assume one Protestant view.
ortho.mortal_and_venial_sin: Orthodox speak of sin and passions, grave sins that separate from the Eucharist, without a neat mortal and venial code. Catholics use that code for Confession and communion. Pastoral outcome can look similar.
protestant.mortal_and_venial_sin: Usually rejected as a Catholic invention; sin is sin. Some speak of willful versus unintentional sin. Loss of salvation depends on the perseverance doctrine they hold.
ortho.total_depravity: Corruption is real; total depravity as Reformed teach it is denied. Image of God remains a basis for synergy. Catholic not totally corrupt matches Orthodox protest.
protestant.total_depravity: If Reformed, yes; if Wesleyan or humanist mainline, no. The term is a Reformed slogan. Catholics should not paste it on all Protestants.
ortho.scripture: Holy Scripture is the heart of Tradition. Catholics say something very similar. The difference is which Church reads it truly.
protestant.scripture: The Bible is the Word of God and final written authority. Catholic Sacred Scripture is never alone. Inspiration is shared language.
ortho.canon: A slightly broader Old Testament than the Catholic list in some churches. No Trent-style single list universally dogmatized in the same way. Large overlap.
oriental_ortho.canon: Canons vary; Ethiopian is notably larger. Catholics should not assume the Tridentine list. All include the core proto-canon.
protestant.canon: Sixty-six books. Deuterocanon excluded. This is the clearest printed difference on a Catholic Bible's table of contents.
ortho.inspiration: The Spirit spoke through the authors and still speaks in the Church's reading. Catholics agree. Verbal-plenary theories are less scholasticized.
protestant.inspiration: Often verbal inspiration of the autographs. Catholic Dei Verbum is both/and: truly human authors, truly God. Evangelical theories can be stricter on wording.
ortho.inerrancy: Scripture is true; modern inerrancy debates are Western. Catholics have a nuanced inerrancy. Orthodox emphasize liturgical truth more than apologetic inerrancy.
protestant.inerrancy: Varies from strict Evangelical inerrancy to mainline historical criticism. Catholic position is neither fundamentalist nor skeptical. Always specify the Protestant camp.
ortho.hermeneutics: The Fathers, liturgy, and council interpret Scripture. Private interpretation apart from the Church is suspect. Catholic Magisterium is a more centralized version of the same instinct.
protestant.hermeneutics: Grammatical-historical method and individual study, with tradition as a helper at most. Magisterium is rejected. This produces both literacy and fragmentation.
ortho.magisterium: No papal Magisterium; the mind of the Church in synod and fathers. Catholics locate a visible living teaching office. Orthodox we have no pope is the contrast they themselves draw.
protestant.magisterium: Teaching authority is ministerial and reformable. Confessions and pastors teach but can err. Catholic infallible Magisterium is denied.
ortho.church: The Church is the visible Orthodox communion, theandric, eucharistic. Catholics say the same of the Catholic Church. Both claim to be the one Church of the Creed.
protestant.church: The church is the congregation of the faithful, sometimes distinguished as invisible and visible. Catholic Church is a visible sacrament of communion. Protestant church can mean denomination or local assembly.
lds.church: The restored Church with living prophets. Catholic and Protestant bodies are extra-Restoration. True church is a present organization.
ortho.one_true_church: The Orthodox Church is the one holy catholic and apostolic Church. Catholics make the parallel claim. Official dialogues try to express remaining communion without erasing the claim.
protestant.one_true_church: Often the invisible company of all true believers; no single visible organization is the one true church. This relativizes both Catholic and Orthodox claims. Some restorationists are the Protestant exceptions.
ortho.marks_of_the_church: One, holy, catholic, apostolic—applied to Orthodoxy. Catholics apply the four marks to the Catholic Church. The list is shared from the Creed.
protestant.marks_of_the_church: Lutheran marks: gospel purely preached and sacraments rightly administered. Catholic four marks are Creedal and institutional. Different checklists.
ortho.visible_and_invisible_church: The Church is visible; a purely invisible church is a Protestant idea Orthodox reject. Catholics agree the Church is visible. Both criticize the invisible-church theory as inadequate.
protestant.visible_and_invisible_church: A standard Reformation device to explain a mixed visible church and a pure elect people. Catholics do not make this the primary distinction. It protects assurance and explains hypocrisy without a papal church.
ortho.ecumenism: Orthodox ecumenism is cautious; some see the WCC as a danger, others engage Rome seriously. Catholic Vatican II ecumenism is more official and developed. Sister churches language appears in Catholic documents toward Orthodox.
protestant.ecumenism: From organic-union schemes to Evangelical networks. Catholic goal is full visible communion including Peter. Protestant unity can stop at mutual recognition.
ortho.schism: Schism is breaking eucharistic communion. 1054 and later ruptures are read as Roman departure. Catholics read the same history as Eastern separation. The word is shared; the culprit is not.
protestant.schism: Division is lamented; sometimes blamed on Rome, sometimes accepted as inevitable until the eschaton. Catholic schism is a canonical crime against unity. Protestants rarely use the canonical definition.
ortho.priesthood: Ministerial priesthood in bishops and presbyters offers the bloodless sacrifice. Catholics agree in substance. Orthodox reject a papal apex to that priesthood.
protestant.priesthood: Priesthood of all believers plus ministers; no sacrificing priests. Catholic ministerial priesthood is the offense. Priest in Protestant use often just means pastor.
ortho.episcopacy: The bishop is the essential minister of unity and Eucharist in his city. Catholics agree and add the pope as bishop of bishops. Orthodox synod of equals around a patriarch is the alternative geometry.
anglican.episcopacy: Historic episcopate is a mark of Anglican identity. Catholic non-recognition of orders complicates the claim. Functionally bishops govern dioceses much as Catholic bishops do.
methodist.episcopacy: Methodist bishops are superintendents; in many bodies they are not in historic apostolic succession as Catholics reckon it. The title is governmental. Sacramental character is not Catholic.
protestant.episcopacy: Some have bishops, many do not. The office is optional or even suspect. Catholic episcopacy is of divine institution.
ortho.priesthood_authority: Priestly power comes through Orthodox ordination and communion. Catholics speak of sacred power in Orders. Mutual non-recognition of the fullness of the other's communion is the wound.
protestant.priesthood_authority: Authority is ministerial, derived from the Word and the church's call. No ontological priestly power. Catholic sacred power is denied.
ortho.papacy: The Pope of Rome is a patriarch who, in Orthodox eyes, left the communion and claimed too much. Catholics see the successor of Peter. Honor is granted to the ancient see; current office is not accepted as defined.
protestant.papacy: The papacy is a human institution, sometimes identified with antichrist in older confessions, more politely declined today. Catholic papal dogmas are rejected.
ortho.liturgical_calendar: A rich year of fasts and feasts, often on the Julian calendar for Pascha. Catholics have a parallel year on the Gregorian calendar. Feasts of the Lord and the Theotokos structure time as they do for Catholics.
anglican.liturgical_calendar: The church year is kept with more or less fullness. Catholics will recognize Advent, Lent, Easter. Lesser Catholic saints' days may be absent.
protestant.liturgical_calendar: Many Evangelicals keep only Christmas and Easter, if those. The Catholic year is seen as extra-biblical. Calendar is adiaphora.
ortho.sunday_worship: The Lord's Day is the day of Resurrection and Eucharist. Catholics agree. Saturday evening vigils may fulfill the feast as in Catholic anticipation.
protestant.sunday_worship: Sunday worship is near-universal except among Sabbatarians. Obligation is moral and customary, not a canonical Sunday Mass precept. The Lord's Day name is shared.
ortho.fasting: Long and physically serious fasts, Great Lent, weekly Wednesday and Friday. Catholic Latin fasting is milder today. Orthodox fasts are a main engine of the year.
oriental_ortho.fasting: Often still more demanding, especially Ethiopian. Catholic readers should not equate contemporary Latin Friday abstinence with these regimens. Fasting is identity.
protestant.fasting: Optional spiritual discipline. No binding seasons for most. Catholic precepts of fast and abstinence are a church law Protestants do not have.
lds.fasting: Monthly fast Sunday with fast offerings for the poor. Comparable to Catholic almsgiving tied to fast. Less calendrically complex than Orthodox Lent.
ortho.sacred_music: Unaccompanied chant is the ideal in many churches. Catholic music includes chant plus instruments and congregational hymnody. Text and mode carry theology.
protestant.sacred_music: Hymns and now praise songs are the Protestant gift to world Christianity. Catholic liturgy has absorbed many hymns. The hymn-sermon-hymn pattern is a Protestant shape.
ortho.instrumental_music: Traditional Orthodox liturgy is a cappella. Instruments are a Latin or Protestant feel for many Orthodox. Catholic organs are not their norm.
protestant.instrumental_music: Generally accepted. Restorationist a cappella is the exception. No Catholic issue here.
ortho.preaching: The homily unfolds the mystery in the Liturgy. Catholics have the same ideal. Preaching is not the Protestant-length center of the service.
protestant.preaching: The sermon is often the main event. Catholic Mass remains centered on Eucharist even when preaching is strong. Protestant churches can be lecture halls around a pulpit.
reformed.preaching: The preached Word is a means of grace, almost sacramental in function. Catholic preaching serves the sacrament. Reformed dignity of the pulpit is very high.
ortho.prayer: Liturgical offices, the Jesus Prayer, intercession of saints. Catholic prayer is a sibling world. Personal prayer is still inside the Church's prayer.
protestant.prayer: Direct address to God, often extemporaneous. No required office. Invocation of saints is excluded.
ortho.intercession_of_saints: The saints pray for us; we ask them to pray. Catholics agree. This is not latria.
oriental_ortho.intercession_of_saints: Same practice. Shared with Catholics against Protestant critique.
protestant.intercession_of_saints: Prayer is to God alone; asking saints is seen as mediation that rivals Christ. Catholics answer that it is request for prayer, like asking a friend.
ortho.theosis: The central Orthodox name for salvation: becoming partakers of the divine nature by the energies. Catholic divinization in the Fathers is the closest analogue. Created grace versus uncreated energies remains the academic gap.
oriental_ortho.theosis: Deification is also a patristic theme. Palamite technicalities may be thinner. Goal of union with God is shared with Catholics.
protestant.theosis: Some recent Protestants retrieve theosis as union with Christ. It is not the ordinary Reformation word. Justification language still dominates.
ortho.salvation: Salvation is healing and theosis, already and not yet. Catholic justification-sanctification-glory can express it in Latin steps. Are you saved is still the wrong question pastorally.
ortho.communion: Holy Communion is the body and blood of Christ in the Divine Liturgy. Catholics agree on Real Presence. Leavened bread and communion from the chalice for infants after baptism differ from ordinary Latin practice.
ortho.real_presence: The gifts become the body and blood; Orthodox often decline to define the change as transubstantiation. Catholics define the change. Realism is shared; Aristotelian explanation is Latin.
baptist.real_presence: Memorial or symbolic presence. Catholic dogma is denied. The supper remembers; it does not contain.
protestant.real_presence: The whole spectrum. Always ask which Protestant. The word real is used even by some who mean only spiritual.
ortho.eucharistic_sacrifice: The Liturgy is a bloodless sacrifice making present Christ's offering. Catholics agree. This is a major point of Orthodox-Catholic closeness against most Protestantism.
protestant.eucharistic_sacrifice: The supper is not a sacrifice offered for the living and the dead. Memorial of a finished sacrifice. Catholic Mass is rejected on this point.
ortho.sacraments: Holy Mysteries, not always strictly numbered at seven, though seven is commonly listed. Catholic seven are the Latin numbering of the same idea. Mystery emphasizes ineffability.
protestant.sacraments: Usually two: baptism and supper. Catholic seven are reduced. Ordinance weakens the grace-claim.
baptist.sacraments: Two ordinances, not sacraments that work by the rite. Symbol and obedience. Catholic ex opere operato is rejected.
protestant.glorification: Final redemption of the body and entrance into glory. Catholic glorification includes the beatific vision. The last step of the Protestant ordo salutis.
protestant.offices_of_christ: Prophet, priest, and king as a teaching scheme. Catholics can adopt it. It structures Protestant preaching about Christ's work.
ortho.gifts_of_the_spirit: Charismata in the life of the Church, discerned in community and monastic tradition. Catholics have a similar discernment. Pentecostal display is less the Orthodox criterion.
protestant.gifts_of_the_spirit: Spiritual gifts for ministry; lists from Paul. Cessationists limit the sign gifts. Catholic confirmation gifts plus Pauline charisms cover the same biblical material.
protestant.tongues: A gift of languages, often judged rare or ceased. Catholic charismatic renewal practices tongues. Reformation caution about disorder remains.
reformed.tongues: Typically cessationist. Tongues belonged to the apostolic founding. Catholic openness to the gift looks like enthusiasm to this tradition.
protestant.continuationism: The charismatic question splits Evangelicals and others. Catholics are soft continuationists with hierarchical discernment. There is no single Protestant answer.
pentecostal.continuing_revelation: Prophecy and words of knowledge occur, tested by Scripture. Not an open canon of new books in most Pentecostal churches. Catholic private revelation is the nearer analogue than LDS scripture.
protestant.open_canon: The canon is closed. No Book of Mormon, no Ellen White as scripture. Catholic closure is shared against restorationist openness.
protestant.continuing_revelation: Public revelation is closed; Scripture is sufficient. Prophecy today, if allowed, cannot add dogma. Catholic public revelation likewise ended; the difference is Tradition and Magisterium, not a living prophet writing scripture.
protestant.restoration: Most Protestants do not claim a total restoration after total loss; they claim a reformation of an erring church. Restorationists and LDS do claim more. Catholic indefectibility opposes both radical restoration and the idea that the medieval Church ceased to be the Church.
protestant.temples: The body is the temple; church buildings are meeting houses, not temples of sacrifice. Catholic church buildings are sacred spaces with reserved Eucharist. LDS temples are a third thing.
protestant.spirit_world: Hades or Sheol as the place of the dead, often split into comfort and misery. LDS spirit world with missionary work is more elaborate. Catholic particular judgment is more definitive.
protestant.marriage: A covenant blessed by God, usually not a sacrament of the seven. Catholic sacramentality and indissolubility are stronger. Pastoral blessing is common.
protestant.divorce: Many allow divorce and remarriage for adultery or abandonment, sometimes more broadly. Catholic ratified consummated marriage cannot be dissolved. Protestant pastors often bless second marriages Catholics would not.
ortho.divorce: Economia permits divorce and limited remarriage. This is the great practical difference from Catholic tribunals that declare nullity rather than dissolve. Both try to be pastoral; the theology of bond differs.
lds.divorce: Civil divorce exists; cancellation of sealing is a separate ecclesiastical act. Catholic annulment addresses validity from the start. Sealing cancellation has no Catholic twin.
protestant.contraception: Generally permitted within marriage. Catholic teaching forbids artificial contraception. This is a live moral divide with most of Protestantism.
ortho.contraception: Orthodox practice varies by bishop and confessors; some allow contraception in a marriage for serious reasons, others are stricter. There is no exact Humanae vitae text. Catholics will find less uniformity.
protestant.sexual_ethics: Historic Protestant ethics match Catholic teaching on adultery and, until recently, on homosexual acts; many mainline bodies have revised that. Evangelical ethics remain closer to Catholic conclusions. Always distinguish mainline from Evangelical.
ortho.sexual_ethics: Chastity in marriage and celibacy in monastic life; homosexual acts are sins. Close to Catholic moral teaching. Pastoral economia exists without changing the rule as some Western Protestants have.
protestant.headship: Ranges from complementarian to egalitarian. Catholic complementarity is not identical to Evangelical complementarianism. Headship language is Pauline and disputed.
ortho.headship: The husband is head of the wife as Christ is head of the Church, read liturgically and iconically. Women do not preside at the altar. Catholic readers will find this familiar and less internally polarized than Protestantism.
lds.headship: The husband presides in the home in council with his wife; priesthood is male. Catholic family headship talk exists in older texts; contemporary Catholic emphasis is mutual submission and equal dignity.
protestant.mormon_label: Protestants commonly say Mormon for Latter-day Saints and often treat the movement as a separate religion. Official LDS preference is Latter-day Saint. The label in Protestant polemic can be dismissive.
ortho.roman_catholic_label: Orthodox often say Roman Catholic or Latins to stress that catholicity is not Rome's property. Catholics hear Roman as a rite or a slight. For Orthodox, they themselves are the Catholic Church.
protestant.roman_catholic_label: Protestants say Roman Catholic to distinguish from the Creed's catholic church they also claim. Catholics prefer Catholic without qualifier. The adjective flags the papacy.
ortho.separated_brethren: Orthodox more often say heterodox than separated brethren. The Catholic Vatican II phrase is warmer than typical Orthodox official speech. Recognition of Catholic baptism varies in Orthodox practice.
protestant.separated_brethren: Protestants do not use this Catholic phrase for themselves. They may call Catholics a denomination or, in older polemic, a false church. Evangelical other believers depends on a born-again test.
ortho.true_church_claim: The Orthodox Church is the Church. Catholics make the mirror claim. This is the ecclesiological standoff.
oriental_ortho.incarnation: The Word became flesh; miaphysite wording still intends a full Incarnation. Catholics confess the same mystery at Chalcedon. Recent joint declarations stress agreement.
ortho.incarnation: The enfleshment of the Word is the foundation of icons, theosis, and liturgy. Catholic dogma matches. Emphasis on deification of the flesh is very strong.
protestant.incarnation: God became man—Chalcedon for the orthodox. Some liberal Protestants mythologize the doctrine. Confessional Protestantism is with the Catholic Creed here.
ortho.virgin_birth: Confessed in the Creed and hymns. Catholic dogma agrees. It is not isolated from ever-virginity as it often is in Protestantism.
protestant.virgin_birth: A test of orthodoxy among Evangelicals; sometimes denied in liberal Protestantism. Catholics define virginal conception. Perpetual virginity is the extra Catholic article.
ortho.preexistence_of_christ: Eternal generation: begotten of the Father before all ages. Catholic dogma agrees. This is not LDS premortal existence among spirits.
protestant.preexistence_of_christ: The eternal Son became incarnate. Shared with Catholics against Arian and adoptionist views. Eternal generation language is more patristic than some Evangelical speech, which may simply say Jesus is God.
ortho.father: The unoriginate Father is the source of the Son and the Spirit. Catholic Trinitarian theology agrees on the Father's monarchy more than popular Western piety sometimes shows. Palamite and Cappadocian frames dominate.
protestant.father: Heavenly Father, first Person of the Trinity in orthodox Protestantism. Address in prayer is often to the Father through the Son. Shared with Catholic liturgy of the Mass.
ortho.holy_spirit: The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, is worshiped and glorified with the Father and the Son. Catholics add Filioque. Personhood is shared against Witnesses.
protestant.holy_spirit: The third Person, Holy Spirit or Holy Ghost. Pentecostals intensify experience. Catholic dogma of personhood is shared with Trinitarian Protestants.
ortho.trinity: One God in three hypostases, the tri-hypostatic God. Catholic Trinity is the same mystery with Filioque tension. This is not LDS Godhead of three beings.
oriental_ortho.trinity: Holy Trinity confessed with the ancient creeds they receive. Shared with Catholics. Filioque is not in their Symbol.
protestant.trinity: One God in three persons—the Nicene faith of orthodox Protestantism. Unitarian and Oneness groups are the Protestant-adjacent exceptions. Catholic and Protestant Trinitarians mean the same core dogma.
lds.trinity: The Godhead is three distinct beings, one in purpose. Catholics call this a denial of consubstantial Trinity. Trinity is the wrong word for what LDS teach; they often say so themselves.
protestant.means_of_grace: Word, prayer, sacraments or ordinances. Catholic sacraments are more densely ontological. The phrase itself is especially Wesleyan and Lutheran.
nazarene.baptism_in_the_spirit: The Church of the Nazarene inherits Holiness second-blessing language of entire sanctification more than Pentecostal tongues. Catholics should hear a crisis of holiness, not Confirmation and not required glossolalia.
salvation_army.baptism_in_the_spirit: The Salvation Army is Holiness in ethos and does not even practice water baptism or the Lord's Supper as ordinances. Spirit-filled holiness is the accent. Catholic sacramental initiation has no Army counterpart.
wesleyan.baptism_in_the_spirit: Wesleyan churches treat entire sanctification as a second definite work. Catholic growth in charity is analogous in goal, not in the two-stage crisis map.
